articles.title: Validating log data indicators of acquiring information in critical online reasoning using eye-tracking data
articles.authors: Jannick Illmann; Yavuz Dinc; Carolin Hahnel; Jochen Kuhn; Stefan Küchemann; Verena Ruf; Maruschka Weber; Frank Goldhammer
articles.abstract: Log data can provide opportunities to measure digital skills. However, the interpretation of log data-based indicators comes with a degree of uncertainty. Eye-tracking data can be used to gain convergent validity for log data-based indicators. We illustrate this approach for Online Information Acquisition (OIA), a facet of Critical Online Reasoning, examining four indicators in 26 students completing an online information task. We defined Areas of Interest around snippets on search engine results pages (SERPs) and assessed correlations between indicators and eye-tracking metrics. Results varied by indicator, with time and scrolling on SERPs being positively associated with the median number of snippets fixated, while other indicators were not significantly associated with corresponding metrics. One indicator could not be assessed as it showed no variation in the sample. Findings provide preliminary evidence for a subset of OIA indicator interpretations and underlines the importance of validation when employing log data-based indicators.

articles.title: The Quantitative Psychologist Is Dead, Long Live the Quantitative Psychologist
articles.authors: Sacha Epskamp
articles.abstract:
Much of what quantitative psychologists publish consists of developing statistical methods, implementing them in software, and evaluating them in simulation studies. I argue that artificial intelligence (AI) can already do much of this work, and that its share will only grow. The quantitative psychologist has always been a jack of all trades, combining programming, statistics, and psychological knowledge without being a master of any one of them. AI is now the better jack of all trades. When methods become cheap, value moves to what AI cannot supply and to what it newly makes possible. I describe three directions: collecting trustworthy data from real people, formalizing psychological theory now that computational modeling is within reach of any researcher, and rethinking methodological education
so that students learn to judge the analyses that AI will run for them. The
specialist role built around producing methods for others will fade, while
quantitative thinking spreads through all of psychology.

articles.title: Determining the perceived utility and veracity of online product reviews: the Consumer Review Evaluation Model (CREM)
articles.authors: Michelle Walther; Sina Frerichs; Steven James Watson; Alexander Boden; Marielle Stel
articles.abstract: When shopping online consumers are frequently confronted with fake reviews. The consequences for the consumers are purchasing flawed, low-quality or even dangerous products. Therefore, to develop effective countermeasures, we need to understand how consumers evaluate the veracity of reviews when making product choices. Thus far, attempts to develop theories about how consumers evaluate review veracity have been based on laboratory or retrospective studies. Therefore, we used thinking-aloud methodology with interactive researcher prompting to more directly observe consumer decision-making regarding the evaluation of consumer reviews. We observed that participants use consumer reviews as a source of information about products. We identified three interrelated judgements in participants’ evaluation of online reviews: review relevance, reviewer credibility, and perceived review veracity. During each judgement participants alternated between heuristic and more systematic processing of deception cues, such as wording, depending on the level of suspicion they trigger. If an evaluation indicated that a review is irrelevant, unbelievable, or untrue, it was not used in the purchase decision process. We integrated our findings from the directly observed decision-making process with existing theory to create an overarching model of human perception of review veracity within the context of an authentic shopping simulation.

articles.title: Predictive Significance Testing: A Complement to Coefficient Significance in Confirmatory Linear Regression
articles.authors: Gyeongcheol Cho
articles.abstract: Across disciplines, linear regression is used to examine hypothesized effects of treatments, interventions and other exposures. Conventional significance tests ask whether population regression coefficients are zero, but do not directly assess the size or practical importance of these effects. A different question is whether estimated effects improve predictions for new observations. An effect can be nonzero yet fail to improve prediction when uncertainty in its estimated coefficient outweighs the predictor's unique signal. Here we introduce predictive significance testing to answer this question within a prespecified linear regression model. We measure the change in expected prediction error when a predictor's fitted contribution is removed at prediction time, without refitting the model. This differs from earlier comparisons of separately estimated forecasting models. Under specified assumptions, we derive an unbiased estimator and a predictive p value that is exactly calibrated at the boundary of no net predictive benefit. We also derive nonzero, sample-size-dependent thresholds for familiar regression effect-size measures that distinguish positive from negative predictive contributions. Simulations support the procedure's statistical performance, and an empirical illustration identifies a predictor that is coefficient-significant but not predictively significant. Together, these results distinguish evidence for a nonzero regression effect from evidence that its estimate improves prediction.

articles.title: Ideological Polarization of Moral Sentiment and Framing in US Media: A Multi-Textual Analysis of the Israel–Hezbollah Conflict
articles.authors: Faiqal Dima Hanif; Haidar Buldan Thontowi
articles.abstract: This study aims to detect polarization of moral sentiment based on ideology in United States left- and right-wing media through moral sentiment analysis and topic modeling in the context of the Israel–Hezbollah (Lebanon) conflict. Moral sentiment analysis was conducted using the extended Moral Foundation Dictionary, followed by a two-tailed independent samples t-test to examine moral sentiment differences between the two media groups. Additionally, topic modeling was employed to explore dominant themes across the articles. The findings indicate that both groups of media exhibit negative moral sentiment toward the conflict; however, left-wing outlets demonstrate a higher degree of negative moral sentiment compared to their right-wing counterparts. Additionally, distinct topical patterns emerged, including themes related to refugees, ceasefire, and terrorist threat. These results provide empirical evidence of moral judgement polarization in US media coverage, particularly in moral sentiment expression and topic framing, as shaped by ideological orientation.

articles.title: Why don’t web survey panelists complete a survey? An analysis of response refusal and discontinuation
articles.authors: Tai Kurosawa
articles.abstract: Not all participants complete web surveys distributed by web research companies. Some refuse to participate in the survey, whereas others discontinue their responses. This study examined the extent of similarity in the reasons for refusal and discontinuation among research company panelists, as well as the associations between refusal and discontinuation and demographic information and sense of busyness. In Study 1, data from 500 participants from a research company were analyzed. In Study 2, data from 600 participants from a research company were analyzed. The results showed that a large number of surveys being distributed was associated with a higher response rate, and the importance of the factors of refusal and discontinuation varied across groups. The findings are discussed with reference to the leverage-salience theory.

articles.title: Audience engagement in live and recorded performance: a social liveness perspective
articles.authors: Robin Ren; Joseph Devlin; John S Hogan; Jorina von Zimmermann; Helen Nuttall; Daniel C. Richardson
articles.abstract: The best memories in life are often collective, from the roar of a stadium to the applause in a concert hall. The value of those moments can be seen in ratings of engagement, feelings of social affiliation, and synchronies in behaviour and autonomic arousal. But what exactly produces the value of the collective experience of a performance? Is it the presence of performers (physical liveness), the presence of other audience members (social liveness), or the fact they are sharing a stimulus? We looked at a range of collective experiences from live theatre to public cinemas to small group viewing in which we varied the two dimensions of liveness and tracked engagement through physiological synchrony. Our goal was to explore some of the many elements that contribute to liveness and engagement. We found that higher liveness, whether physical or social, fostered higher audience engagement and elevated heart rate synchrony. However, co-present pairs were not always more synchronised than pseudo-pairs who watched the same narrative stimuli at different times, suggesting that collective entrainment is not a uniform consequence of ‘being together’. We argue that while many dimensions of sociality might contribute to social liveness, understanding how they combine, how they are balanced with the narrative stimuli to foster collective entrainment without being distracted is the key to creating an engaging collective experience.

articles.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between psychological monitor competency and mental health literacy: A reassessment of Guo et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Guo et al. recently reported statistically significant links in a cross-lagged panel network (CLPN) model and interpreted these findings as evidence that psychological monitor competency reinforces mental health literacy among university psychological monitors. However, methodological research has shown that cross-lagged estimates may emerge as artifacts of model specification rather than reflecting genuine prospective influence. To examine the robustness of the reported findings, we reanalyzed the data used by Guo et al. using several alternative analytic approaches. Across specifications, estimated associations varied considerably in both magnitude and direction, with positive, negative, and nonsignificant effects all observed. Meta-analytic aggregation of estimates across models generally yielded effects that were not statistically different from zero. These results indicate that the conclusions advanced by Guo et al. may not be robust and that the apparent prospective associations could be attributable to methodological artifacts. Strong developmental interpretations are therefore not warranted on the basis of the available evidence. We recommend that observational findings, including cross-lagged effects, be evaluated across multiple defensible modeling approaches before substantive conclusions are drawn.

articles.title: Covert control over the real-time dynamics of human interactions with Ducksoup
articles.authors: Pablo Arias Sarah; Guillaume Denis; Philippe schyns; Rachael Jack; Petter Johansson; Lars Hall; Jean-Julien Aucouturier
articles.abstract:
Uncovering how facial and vocal signals shape social interactions is difficult because researchers
cannot control how humans behave during free conversations. Here we demonstrate that recent
advances in AI-based transformation filters enable researchers to have covert experimental control
over the real-time dynamics of social interactions. We introduce Ducksoup, a scientific
videoconference platform that allows researchers to collect social interaction experiments online,
realistically transform participants' faces and voices in real time mid-conversation, record the
synchronized interactions and extract multimodal time series from recordings for analysis. In a
preregistered experiment (N = 64 participants), we replicate recent laboratory findings in a fully
online setup: artificially aligning participants’ smiles increased mutual enjoyment while remaining
undetected. The paradigm also revealed feedback effects on participants’ spontaneous facial, vocal
and verbal behavior. By combining the ecological validity of free interactions with experimental
control and scalable data collection, Ducksoup turns natural conversations into a causal
experimental paradigm for psychology and neuroscience.

articles.title: The Unappreciated Helper: When an AI Facilitation Agent Improves Group Efficiency Despite Poorer User Perceptions
articles.authors: Nicolas Michinov; Marinette Bouet; Eric Jamet; Axel Mascaro; Muriel Noël; Albane Pechard; Farouk Toumani; Zineddine Zahouani; Estelle Michinov
articles.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence make it possible to embed AI facilitation agents in collaborative settings, where they can deliver real-time recommendations based on ongoing group discussions. This experimental study examined how group members perceive a collaborative platform with or without such an agent and evaluated the agent’s effects on group communication and performance. A total of 187 undergraduate psychology students collaborated in 50 groups of three or four members on a digital platform with a synchronous text chat. Groups were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (25 groups per condition): with an AI facilitation agent (n = 96 participants) that encouraged information sharing when exchanges were insufficient, or without the agent (n = 91 participants). Participants rated the platform’s acceptability, perceived support, sense of intrusion, and affective reactions. Participants in the AI condition rated the platform as less acceptable and less supportive, but not more intrusive or unpleasant. Nevertheless, groups assisted by the agent were more efficient, completing the task faster with less communicative effort. Descriptive analyses of group interactions in the three minutes before and after the agent’s interventions showed a shift from providing information toward requesting information, expressing opinions, and agreeing, without change in overall interaction volume. These findings reveal a gap between objective performance and subjective perceptions, highlighting the need to design AI agents that improve group efficiency while fostering members’ sense of support and acceptance.

articles.title: On the Stability of Individual Differences in the Truth Effect
articles.authors: Selina Zajdler; Lena Nadarevic; Markus Wache; Martin Schnuerch
articles.abstract: Repeated information is judged as more valid than new information, a robust cognitive phenomenon known as the truth effect. Individuals differ in the extent to which they show the effect, but results regarding the covariation of these individual differences with dispositional variables have been inconsistent. To address these inconsistencies, we focus on the methodological prerequisites necessary to find such associations: that individual differences in the truth effect can be reliably measured and that they are stable over time. We address both prerequisites across four studies using a Bayesian hierarchical model and Bayes factor model comparison. We first reanalyze three existing datasets and find mixed evidence for stability: one dataset yields inconclusive results alongside low reliability, another provides evidence for stability across sessions, and a third provides evidence for stability across retention intervals, though with considerable uncertainty regarding the magnitude. In a new experiment (N = 196, L = 50 trials per condition) designed in accordance with previously established experimental design recommendations, we then assess stability both across sessions and retention intervals within a single study. We demonstrate that individual truth effects can be reliably measured within a single session, directly validating these design recommendations, and find strong evidence that individual differences covary substantially across two sessions and retention intervals. Together, these findings lay the foundation for future research on individual differences in the truth effect and how they relate to personality traits, cognitive abilities, and other dispositional variables.

articles.title: Corruption Perceptions Predict Conspiracy Beliefs More Strongly in Low-Corruption Contexts
articles.authors: Sinan Alper; Ayşenur Düzgün; Eylül Deran Atalay; Onurcan Yilmaz
articles.abstract: Perceptions of institutional corruption are consistently associated with conspiracy beliefs, yet their predictive value may depend on the institutional context in which they arise. We propose a context-sensitive account in which corruption perceptions and distrust in institutions are more strongly predictive of conspiracy thinking in relatively clean societies than in highly corrupt ones. In Study 1 (N = 3,401), an illustrative two-country comparison in which recruitment mode and sample composition differ alongside corruption, perceived corruption was more strongly associated with conspiracy beliefs in the UK than in Türkiye, a higher-corruption context, even after accounting for theoretically-relevant individual differences. Study 2 (N = 34,356 across 20 European countries) extended this contextual moderation through a partial replication using multilevel models and institutional distrust as a proxy for perceived corruption, a related construct. The interaction with institutional distrust remained consistent across alternative models, country-level covariates, and tests of measurement invariance. These findings suggest that the belief that institutions are corrupt (Study 1) and institutional distrust (Study 2) might carry different implications depending on institutional context. By integrating individual perceptions with institutional conditions, this research advances a context-sensitive account of conspiracy beliefs.

articles.title: Stereotypes of Epistemic Sources and Conspiracy Beliefs: The Primacy of Perceived Morality
articles.authors: Deniz Bayramoğlu; Sinan Alper
articles.abstract: The present study examines how stereotypes of epistemic sources predict conspiracy beliefs through the lens of the Stereotype Content Model (SCM). Two studies with nationally representative samples from the United Kingdom (N = 290) and the United States (N = 289) assessed perceptions of doctors, academics, journalists, and government officials in terms of sociability, morality, competence, and assertiveness, alongside general and profession-specific conspiracy beliefs. Correlational and random forest regression analyses showed that perceived morality was the most consistent and robust predictor across professions, with lower perceived morality associated with higher conspiracy beliefs. Other dimensions showed more context-dependent associations: Competence occasionally contributed, particularly for academics; sociability varied across professions; and assertiveness was generally a weak predictor. These findings suggest that conspiracy beliefs regarding epistemic authorities are more consistently associated with perceived moral character than with perceived expertise, although competence also played a role, particularly for academics.

articles.title: Environmental Sensitivity Moderates Negative Affect During Brief Virtual Nature and Urban Exposure in Japanese Young Adults
articles.authors: Hiromi Nakadaira; Yuichi KIKURAKU; Shuhei Iimura
articles.abstract: Immersive virtual reality offers a way to experience natural settings when direct access to nature is limited. We investigated short-term affective and physiological responses to virtual natural and crowded urban environments and whether these responses differed by environmental sensitivity. Fifty-eight Japanese university students aged 18–24 years were randomly assigned to watch a 7-minute head-mounted-display video of a forest and stream (Nature, n = 29) or a crowded urban station (Urban, n = 29). Negative affect and salivary α-amylase activity were measured before and after viewing; heart rate variability was assessed during exposure. Negative affect decreased after nature exposure but increased after urban exposure. The between-condition difference in change was larger at higher levels of environmental sensitivity, driven more clearly by greater negative-affect increases in the urban condition than by sensitivity-related change in the nature condition. No statistically reliable condition difference was detected for salivary α-amylase or during-exposure heart rate variability. These findings suggest that brief immersive virtual environments elicit contrasting short-term affective responses that vary with environmental sensitivity, while physiological effects remain uncertain.

articles.title: The Political is Relational: Political Dissimilarity Predicts Worse Relationship Quality and Likelihood of Breakup
articles.authors: Yitong Zhao; Stephanie Domingo; Noah M. Laskey; Matthew Feinberg; Spike W. S. Lee; Brett Quaid Ford
articles.abstract: Politics is not just about policy—it can become deeply personal, straining relationships between family members, friends, and romantic partners who hold different political views. Extending prior work that mostly focused on romantic relationships in non-representative samples, we tested whether political dissimilarity predicted worse relationship quality across romantic and non-romantic close relationships in a nationally representative U.S. sample (N = 1,075; 45% Republican, 55% Democrat) during a period of heightened political tension around the 2024 U.S. election. In a ten-wave longitudinal study spanning September 2024 to October 2025, greater political dissimilarity predicted worse relationship quality and a 22% higher odds of relationship breakup. These effects were comparable across various sociodemographics and close relationship types, indicating broad generalizability. These findings underscore the widespread relational costs of political dissimilarity: Political divides spill deeply into personal life, eroding the quality and stability of people’s closest ties.

articles.title: Mentalizing across the Antagonism Spectrum: Opposing Associations with Callousness, Aggression, and Dishonesty
articles.authors: Michelle M. Berry; Scott D. Blain; Aisha Linnea Udochi; Muchen Xi; Colin G. DeYoung; Timothy Allen
articles.abstract: Theory of mind, or mentalizing, is the ability to infer what other people think and feel. Deficits in theory of mind are related to many of the interpersonal problems associated with antagonistic forms of psychopathology. Yet some antagonistic behaviors, such as deception, may benefit from accurately anticipating what another person believes. We tested whether three facets of antagonism – callousness, aggression, and dishonesty – showed opposing associations with mentalizing accuracy. Participants recruited online and from a university campus (N = 335) completed self-report measures of normal-range and pathological personality traits and three tasks that required them to reason about characters’ beliefs in stories, classify interactions between animated shapes, and identify mental states from photographs of the eyes. We used target-rotated exploratory structural equation modeling to estimate associations between the three antagonism facets and a latent factor capturing mentalizing across the tasks. Greater callousness and aggression were each associated with lower mentalizing accuracy, both when examined individually and when all three facets were modeled simultaneously. Greater dishonesty was associated with lower mentalizing accuracy when examined on its own, but with higher accuracy after accounting for callousness and aggression. Task-specific estimates generally followed the same directions but varied in magnitude and precision. These findings extend earlier single-task work and suggest that difficulty understanding others’ mental states may be more characteristic of some forms of antagonism than others.

articles.title: Neural Correlates of Partner Comparisons and Their Links to Intimate Partner Aggression
articles.authors: Sydney Kavanaugh; Alexandra Martelli; Samuel James West; Emily Lasko; David Skylan Chester
articles.abstract: People frequently compare themselves to their intimate partners. These partner comparisons are critical for relationship maintenance, with powerful ramifications for intimate partner aggression (IPA) perpetration. However, little is known about the neural correlates of partner comparisons and their relation to IPA perpetration. To address this gap, 96 participants from 49 intimate partner dyads underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and completed a social comparison task, judging their own negative and positive traits against those of their partner and the average person. Participants then reported whether they had any history of IPA perpetration. Consistent with previous findings, participants reported having less negative and more positive traits than others. However, participants’ tendency to compare themselves favorably to others was attenuated for their partners. Partner (> average person) comparisons were linked to heightened activity in the mentalizing network (DMPFC, precuneus, TPJ) and DLPFC, particularly for negative traits. Such DLPFC/DMPFC activity during partner comparisons related to greater IPA perpetration for negative traits and lesser IPA perpetration for positive traits. These findings suggest that recruiting mentalizing and executive control networks during partner comparisons may be meaningfully linked to IPA perpetration, depending on trait valence.

articles.title: Regulating Self-Interest: The Effect of Anodal tDCS over the Right Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex in the Ultimatum Game
articles.authors: Haim Assor; Jonathan slater; Eliran Halali
articles.abstract: In many social situations, a conflict exists between self-interest and social considerations such as fairness and reciprocity. Previous research suggests that self-interested behavior is an automatic response, requiring cognitive control to be regulated. Consistent with this view, neuroeconomics findings implicate the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) in regulating self-interested behavior and implementing social preferences. Whereas prior neuromodulation studies have shown that inhibition or disruption of the rDLPFC increases self-interested behavior, studies examining the effects of enhancing rDLPFC activity have yielded inconsistent results. Moreover, it remains unclear whether such enhancement promotes responses to intentional unfairness alone or also to inequality per se. In the present study, we applied anodal transcranial direct-current stimulation (tDCS) over the rDLPFC to reexamine its causal role in regulating self-interested behavior among ultimatum game responders. In addition, we tested whether this manipulation promotes responses to both intentional unfairness and inequality resulting from an intention-free process. The results show that anodal stimulation increased rejection rates of unfair offers, regardless of whether they were proposed by a human partner or randomly generated by a computer. These findings suggest that rDLPFC activity supports the implementation of social preferences more broadly, promoting both reciprocal fairness and inequality aversion. When considered alongside prior findings demonstrating an opposite effect of anodal stimulation applied to an adjacent lateral prefrontal region using a similar paradigm, the results point to distinct and complementary roles of lateral prefrontal regions in managing the conflict between self-interest and social preferences. We discuss implications for dual-process accounts of social decision-making.

articles.title: “What’s our color? POOR”: Exploring the Consequences of Racism-Conscious Framings of Environmental Exposures
articles.authors: Harrison James Schmitt; Lily Schwartzman; Trevor Scott Lies
articles.abstract: Environmental justice activists increasingly pursue public awareness campaigns to garner support as they face injustice. However, little psychological research has investigated the implications of different framings of recognition justice for collective action. Two experiments with qualitative components test the primary hypothesis that recognition of systemic racism in environmental exposures may represent a double-edged sword. We test implications of racism-conscious framings of inequitable lead exposures on collective action intentions among Black, Latine, and White US residents. Study 1 (n=590) finds that a racism-conscious frame increases anger and systemic knowledge of racism but does not affect collective action intentions, except among highly racially identified White participants, whose collective action intentions decreased after the manipulation. Results of Study 2 (n=703) suggest that a combined racism- and class-conscious frame may prevent (highly-identified) White disengagement from collective action. We discuss addressing environmental injustice through coalition building while acknowledging the double-edged sword of racism-conscious recognition.

articles.title: The Measurement Reliability Crisis in Event-Related Potential Research: Evidence from Bilingual Language Control
articles.authors: Projnya Mojumdar
articles.abstract: Event-related potential (ERP) research exhibits a critical methodological blind spot: inter-condition correlations (ρXY), the parameter that mathematically determines difference wave reliability via the Lord–Novick formula, are systematically unmeasured. Classical Test Theory demonstrates that difference wave reliability is inversely related to ρXY, with high correlations suppressing reliability even when constituent waveforms are psychometrically sound. A purposive examination of four foundational ERP studies in bilingual language switching (2001–2016, Ncitations ≈ 1,575) found that none report difference wave reliability or inter-condition correlations, despite difference waves being the primary dependent variables isolating language control processes. Sensitivity analysis reveals that this vulnerability extends across the entire plausible parameter space: even moderate inter-condition correlations (ρXY = .50–.60) require constituent reliabilities approaching methodological ceilings (ρ = .85–.88) to achieve adequate difference wave reliability (ρDD′ ≥ .70). Because the observed inter-condition correlation is itself capped at √(ρXX′ρYY′), difference wave reliability is bounded between zero and the constituent reliability, and it falls to zero exactly as experimental control drives ρXY toward that ceiling: constituent reliabilities of .85 yield ρDD′ = .50 at ρXY = .70 and ρDD′ = 0 at ρXY = .85. The absence of empirical ρXY measurements means the field cannot determine whether two decades of N2 debate reflect genuine neurocognitive complexity, measurement instability, or both. Three reforms can address this gap: mandatory reporting of difference wave reliability and inter-condition correlations, adoption of Generalizability Theory frameworks, and single-trial analytical methods that avoid categorical subtraction. These principles extend beyond bilingual research to all ERP domains using difference waves. Systematic psychometric verification should precede theoretical elaboration.

articles.title: “Huge if true”: Aspirational believing and the appeal of conspiracy theories
articles.authors: Sander Van de Cruys
articles.abstract:
Why do people believe in conspiracy theories? I propose that part of the answer lies in what our metacognitive feelings track. Curiosity and the aha experience are fallible markers of truth, but good markers of subjective progress: of gaining grip on a problem through one’s own inquiry. This leads to a different view of belief, which I call aspirational believing. People may accept hypotheses on thinner evidence when acting on them promises control, because that action opens new channels for evidence and agency, whether or not the hypothesis is true. In moderation this sustains exploration, but pushed too far, belief stops reacting to evidence. Conspiracy theories are a prime example of this. They turn diffuse, uncontrollable experiences into plots that can be probed and exposed, and their “do
your own research” arcs reliably deliver the felt insights that signal progress. The approach does not require that conspiracy believers experience an unusual need for certainty or control, just that they are optimistically biased in their control expectations (like most of us). I distinguish this account from motivated reasoning, error management and compensatory control accounts, and derive diverging, testable predictions. I close with a tentative remedy: fostering (epistemic and pragmatic) agency may matter more than cleaning up information diets.

articles.title: The cognitive and social origins of randomization devices
articles.authors: Tal Boger; Dorsa Amir
articles.abstract: From throwing dice to reading tea leaves, humans across diverse cultures, eras, and geographies rely on decision aids that produce randomness. What purpose do these aids serve, and why do cultures create them with such regularity? In this Perspective, we unify these seemingly disparate tools as randomization devices, and argue that they culturally evolved to solve two recurrent problems, one cognitive and one social. Specifically, randomization devices produce strong, unpredictable randomness, whereas human cognition does not; and randomization devices externalize decisions in ways that create a social buffer between decision-makers and outcomes. The design of such devices reflects these constraints, even in relation to unique mechanistic features. We focus on one such property — causal opacity — as an important feature of randomization devices that subserves their function and arises in diverse literatures spanning cultural evolution, computer science, and political philosophy. Taken together, we argue that the widespread recurrence of randomization devices reflects widespread cognitive constraints and social demands.

articles.title: The Other Side of Prolific: Ethical Research Guidelines Based on a Mixed Methods Investigation of Prolific Platform Workers’ Experiences
articles.authors: Louis Bachaud; Macken Murphy; Antoine Marie
articles.abstract:
Experimental and survey research is increasingly reliant on crowdsourced
participant recruitment platforms like Prolific. Yet, while Prolific workers are arguably one of the
most well-studied populations in human history, little is known about their actual working
conditions. This preregistered mixed-methods study explores working conditions on Prolific
drawing on different sources: (1) a qualitative inductive analysis of the r/ProlificAC subreddit, a
platform where Prolific workers gather to discuss their experiences; (2) statistics from a survey on
working conditions, labor identity, income, motivations, fraud, and potential grievances of Prolific
workers (n=455); (3) qualitative analyses of open-ended responses to the same survey. Overall,
these analyses reveal an unbalanced power dynamic on the platform, with the workers at a
disadvantage relative to researchers, due to competition between workers, lack of social protection,
hurdles to collective organization, and platform design—logics inherent to the crowdsourcing
model. We also reveal for the first time clear evidence of fraud on the worker side of Prolific,
through a secondary market of trading and faking accounts. Based on these findings, we provide
clear and actionable guidelines for researchers wishing to use the platform in an ethical way. We
also suggest steps for the Prolific company to both ensure data quality and guarantee fair relations
between clients and workers.

articles.title: Convincing Without Conflict? Persuasion and Its Social Costs in Human–AI Conversations About Meat Reduction
articles.authors: Elena Wurth; Georg Ahnert; Ira Elisa Herwig; Ahmed Salem; Markus Strohmaier; Jutta Mata
articles.abstract: Meat consumption in high-income countries exceeds recommendations. Because meals are often shared, conversations can spark meat reduction, yet advocates often remain silent because persuading carries social costs. Generative AI has proven persuasive and could inform such conversations. Drawing on research on persuasion and reactance, we examined how persuasion and its social costs depend on the source of the strategies and on the medium delivering them. In a preregistered 5 × 2 experiment (N = 521), participants discussed a shared meal with a fictional counterpart, either a chatbot or a text-based script. The counterpart used strategies from the behavioral science literature, a large language model, or a generative agent simulation, or did not argue for meat reduction (neutral and placebo controls). Arguing for meat reduction increased intentions and more than quadrupled the odds of choosing a vegetarian dish in both media; arguing for an unrelated sustainability behavior did not shift choice. Persuasion increased perceived threat to freedom but did not reduce liking of the counterpart. AI-derived strategies persuaded as well as literature-based strategies, at no higher social cost. As predicted, the chatbot incurred higher social costs than the text-based dialogue. Studies of AI-based persuasion should assess social costs alongside persuasiveness.

articles.title: AI versus human source attribution and perceived empathy in supportive communication: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: Arthur Bran Herbener; Filip Skjold Thidemann; Caroline Gjørtsvang Kock; Malene Flensborg Damholdt
articles.abstract: Research suggests that people attribute less empathy to supportive communication labelled as AI-generated rather than human-written, but the evidence is mixed, and it is unclear whether the effect varies with how empathy is conceptualized and operationalized. In the present paper, we report a systematic review and meta-analysis of source-attribution effects (human vs. AI) on perceived empathy in supportive communication. A systematic literature search identified 10 records reporting the results of 18 independent studies (N = 13,541). We observed a small source-attribution effect on perceived general empathy (g = 0.41, 95% CI [0.23, 0.58]), cognitive empathy (g = 0.39, 95% CI [0.16, 0.63]), motivational empathy (g = 0.42, 95% CI [0.19, 0.64]), and a moderate effect for affective empathy (g = 0.50, 95% CI [0.19, 0.81]). However, substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies. Alt-hough gender initially emerged as a significant moderator of general perceived empathy, this association was no longer significant after excluding two influential outliers. The analyses also found no statistically significant moderation by age, exposure type (vignette vs. first-person interaction), or supportive setting. Thus, the sources of the substantial between-study heterogeneity remain largely unex-plained. Future research is needed to identify the conditions shaping source-attribution effects on empathy and evaluate whether these effects persist or fade over the course of interactions.

articles.title: Social prioritization of others can be explained by representational  closeness to the self
articles.authors: Meike Scheller; Georgios Velimachitis; Gabrielle Foster; Greesha Yadav
articles.abstract: Visual cognition is shaped not only by sensory input, but also by social relevance. While self-related information is processed preferentially, similar advantages extend to close others. How prioritization rapidly extends to others, however, remains unclear. We propose a framework of ‘representational closeness’, whereby individuals cognitively represented closer to the self, benefit from more efficient processing. Devising three markers – closeness, boundary imprecision, overlap – in a reanalysis of Scheller & Sui (2022, n = 43) and a new experiment (n = 78), we show that this framework explains processing benefits across two domains: friends over strangers, and more over less attractive strangers. Faster and more accurate responses, reduced response variability, and increased self-other confusion tracked representational closeness. These findings suggest that prioritization reflects a general organising principle of social perception through which cognitive resources are dynamically allocated according to social relevance, linking visual processing to the structure of social representation.

articles.title: The State of Play: Methodological Reflections on Phenomenological Psychopathology
articles.authors: Jodie Louise Russell; Lucienne Spencer; Matthew Broome
articles.abstract: In this paper, we reflect on the position of the researcher within the field of phenomenological psychopathology and the ways they can overcome privilege and outsider status in order to more accurately and ethically grasp the structure of disorder experience from the perspective of the person living it. §1 discusses problems incorporating lived experience as well as its challenges within phenomenological psychopathology. §2 introduces the phenomenological notion of play in the work of Husserl and Fink. §3 elaborates on the political and ethical dimensions of play using the work of Lugones, and §4 then discusses how playfulness might be applied in health research to overcome the problems outlined in §1. §5 then gives examples of how play might be utilised within the methodology of phenomenological psychopathology. Overall, we suggest that both researchers and those with lived experience can engage in processes of understanding that can facilitate safe and inclusive interactions through the medium of play.

articles.title: Feasibility of virtual reality in assessing functional communication in persons with aphasia
articles.authors: Marina Ruiter; Vitória Piai; Hilde Bosschers; Mirjam Otters; Lizet van Ewijk; Edward Bosma; Willemijn Josefien Doedens
articles.abstract: Functional communication skills represent important measures in aphasia therapy. Assessing these skills, however, remains challenging. Mainstream pen-and-paper based instruments often elicit indirect rather than direct speech and fail to capture the complex communicative demands encountered in everyday communication situations, limiting their ecological validity and construct validity. The current study explored the feasibility of using immersive Virtual Reality (iVR) to assess functional communication in persons with aphasia. After developing a proof-of-concept version – incorporating the needs and ideas of both speech and language therapists and persons with aphasia - we investigated whether (1) iVR enables a realistic simulation of everyday communication, including its technical feasibility and acceptability for the intended users, and (2)  iVR simulation has added value for functional communication assessment by allowing manipulation of communicative complexity, the elicitation of direct speech, and both verbal and non-verbal aspects of communication to be assessed. The results suggest that it is technically feasible to create iVR environments for the assessment of functional communication in persons with aphasia that are acceptable to (end) users and that enhance the construct validity of functional communication tests. Despite remaining areas for improvement, iVR was found to have a clear added value for assessment purposes.

articles.title: Hierarchical knowledge and skills undermine payoff-biased social learning
articles.authors: Nanda Ramo Jafarian; Björn Lindström; Ingmar Visser; Annemie Ploeger; Pieter van den Berg; Lucas Molleman
articles.abstract: Acquiring skills and knowledge (“traits”) through social learning is central to human development and cultural evolution. Yet it remains unclear how individuals can effectively learn from others when traits form hierarchies, with advanced traits building on more basic ones. We present a model showing that trait hierarchies favour “proximal social learning” where individuals copy others who are only slightly more knowledgeable. In contrast, payoff bias - often assumed to be universally advantageous - performs poorly because it directs learners toward advanced traits they lack the basics for. Our experiments demonstrate that people indeed shift to proximal social learning when conditions favour it. Our results challenge core assumptions of mainstream cultural evolution theory and highlight that trait hierarchies are a key factor shaping human social learning.

articles.title: Risks and Benefits of Neuroticism in Adolescence: Longitudinal Evidence from Population and Clinic-Referred Samples
articles.authors: Larissa Lucia Wieczorek; Eva Bleckmann; Solomiia Myroniuk; Bertus F. Jeronimus; Sanne Booij; Jenny Wagner; Albertine Oldehinkel
articles.abstract:
Background: Neuroticism is known for being linked to detrimental outcomes, but it may also serve beneficial functions in adolescence, where avoiding and protecting oneself from risks becomes crucial. 
Method: We examined potential risks and benefits of neuroticism based on longitudinal data of two samples of Dutch adolescents, one population (n = 2229, 51% female) and one clinic-referred (n = 543, 34% female) sample. Neuroticism was measured with parent-ratings of the temperament facets fear and frustration and used to predict a diverse set of outcomes in the domains lifestyle choices (e.g., substance abuse) and social resources (e.g., social skills) between ages 11 to 19. 
Results: High neuroticism conveyed heightened risk but three key observations refine this picture: (1) fear related to fewer risks than frustration and was additionally linked to benefits regarding better social skills and more prosocial behavior among adolescents in the clinic-referred sample; (2) both fear and frustration were consistently associated with parent-rated social behavior problems across measurement points, while other risk-related associations were less consistent; (3) most links between fear and detrimental outcomes became non-significant after controlling for childhood adversity (e.g., low socioeconomic status, parental divorce). 
Conclusions: Although our results indicate several risk-related effects, we also provide initial evidence that the fear facet of neuroticism can be beneficial in adolescence, especially among youth with a clinical background and in the social domain. We call for more nuanced research studying the potential protective role of neuroticism within high-risk populations.

articles_hidden.title: Frontotemporal and parietal theta and beta synchronization support musical pleasure and motor learning
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander William Albury; Marc Deosdad Díez; Gemma Fàbrega-Camps; Alberto Ara; Josep Marco; Virginia Penhune
articles_hidden.abstract: Music perception and performance involve a broad range of cognitive processes related to prediction, pleasure, and action planning. Each of these processes and behaviours recruit distinct brain areas, and these brain areas must communicate with each other to coordinate complex behaviours such as learning to play an instrument. One theorized mechanism supporting this interregional coordination is synchronization of neural oscillations. Theta- and beta-band activity in particular have been identified as being related to music reward and motor planning, respectively. In this study, we measured oscillatory activity using EEG while non-musicians performed a passive listening task and piano learning task. Using Bayesian regression models, we measured the relationship between intersite theta synchronization and liking ratings, and intersite beta synchronization and motor learning accuracy and asynchrony. Replicating previous research, we found that theta synchronization between right frontotemporal areas was positively associated with participant liking ratings. We also observed long-range theta synchronization between right frontal and parietal areas. In beta, we found that synchronization in right frontotemporal areas was associated with motor learning accuracy, and synchronization in parietomotor areas was associated performance asynchrony. These results provide evidence for the role of theta-band activity in music reward and suggest that processes of evaluation are supported by communication between a broad network of regions in the dorsal and ventral auditory streams. The results also highlight the role of beta-band activity in supporting pitch-to-key mapping and timing accuracy during motor learning in music.

articles_hidden.title: Give-a-number task scoring methods influence the observed number knowledge
articles_hidden.authors: Attila Krajcsi
articles_hidden.abstract: The Give-a-number (GaN) task is used to determine the symbolic number knowledge of children when they initially acquire the meaning of the number words. Precise measurement of number knowledge is essential because even small measured differences in the development process may lead to fundamental theoretical consequences. The task has several variations, and these versions are usually considered equivalent. However, recent works have raised the issue that different versions may classify children differently, which has been partially confirmed. Here, to extend these initial studies, the role of the various scoring methods of the task, that is, how the number knowledge is calculated given the task responses, was investigated. It was found that the scoring method considerably influences the observed number knowledge, and the effects of the various scoring method components are added up. These results demonstrate that the specific scoring method influences the validity and reliability of the measurement. These differences affect the comparability of studies using different methods of the GaN task, and various versions lead to differing observed patterns that, in turn, may lead to differing theoretical conclusions.

articles_hidden.title: Certain Minds in an Uncertain World? Exploring Computational Signatures of Belief Updating in Individuals Holding Radical Attitudes
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Knorr; Nikita Podolin; Alexander Starlinger; Małgorzata Kossowska; Nace Mikus
articles_hidden.abstract: Radical political attitudes have been linked to rigid beliefs, a pattern commonly understood as reflecting motivational processes that promote the defense of valued beliefs and identities. Emerging evidence suggests that this rigidity also manifests in how individuals process politically neutral information, suggesting a domain-general rigid cognitive style. The computational basis of this cognitive style, however, remains largely unknown. We investigated the computational correlates of radical attitudes during learning under uncertainty using a politically neutral predictive-inference task in 462 US adults. Dogmatic intolerance and authoritarianism, two radical-attitude dimensions derived from a battery of political-attitude questionnaires, were both associated with overconfidence. We also found weak evidence that dogmatic intolerance was associated with poorer predictive performance, but no evidence that either radical-attitude factor was associated with impaired metacognitive sensitivity. Computational modelling indicated that dogmatic intolerance, but not authoritarianism, was selectively associated with a more changeable representation of environmental volatility. This raises the possibility that dogmatic-intolerant belief systems are sustained by allowing contradictory experiences to be explained away as changes in the environment rather than as challenges to existing beliefs. Together, these findings suggest that heightened subjective certainty may coexist with more labile representations of environmental regularities, pointing to a computational signature of dogmatic intolerance.

articles_hidden.title: Semantic structure and measurement in large language models for psychopathology and psychometrics
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Raballo; Michele Poletti; Antonio Preti
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reconstruct item-item associations and subscale structure in psychopathology questionnaires from the semantic and sentiment embeddings of item text. Responding to Kambeitz et al. (Nature Mental Health, 2025), this finding extends beyond representation: the linguistic composition of psychometric instruments may help shape the covariance observed in responses, not only reflect latent constructs. Convergent work in semantic psychometrics indicates that item semantics can be used operationally, supporting item-level questionnaire completion from unstructured text, cross-scale prediction, and diagnostic inference. Implications for questionnaire redundancy, instrument harmonization, and language-based adaptive assessment follow. Semantic structure cannot, however, replace empirical validation, clinical judgment, or longitudinal and interventional evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Linguistic Variation in Wrap-Up Effects Reflects Adaptive Sensitivity to Information Structure
articles_hidden.authors: Inbal Kimchi; Amit Avigdor; Leon Hager; Paul van den Broek; Sascha Schroeder; Victor Kuperman; Noam Siegelman
articles_hidden.abstract: The wrap-up effect, i.e., the inflation of reading times on sentence- or clause-final words relative to preceding words, is a robust finding in reading research, typically interpreted to reflect integrative processing of meaning. However, recent cross-linguistic evidence has cast doubt on its generalizability across languages, raising questions about the mechanisms that underlie it. Here, we test an information-theoretic account of the wrap-up effect, according to which the effect reflects readers’ adaptive behavior to where semantic information resides in their written language. We start by showing in a large-scale text reading database (N=1,234 from 20 languages) that there is, in fact, systematic cross-linguistic variation in wrap-up effects. Then, we use sentence-embeddings to quantify languages’ trajectories of semantic informativeness in sentence endings, showing that they closely align with the observed cross-linguistic variability in wrap-up effects. Specifically, languages with increasing informativeness in sentence endings also show canonical wrap-up effects, whereas languages with declining informativeness patterns have no or reversed effects. Lastly, we show that these correlations are driven by readers’ general expectations regarding the structure of their written language. This is revealed by models showing that global (i.e., language-specific mean) informativeness trajectories rather than local (i.e., sentence-level) changes predict the magnitude of the wrap-up effect in a given sentence. Together, these findings provide a novel interpretation of the mechanisms underlying the wrap-up effect, positioning it as a consequence of learning computations that readers use to assimilate their writing system’s structure, thus offering a principled explanation for its cross-linguistic variability.

articles_hidden.title: Automating Reproducibility Checks Using Large Language Models
articles_hidden.authors: Yoel Inbar; David Tannenbaum
articles_hidden.abstract: Computational reproducibility checks are essential to scientific credibility, yet few published papers are ever independently verified, largely because manual checking is labor-intensive and time-consuming. We tested whether an agentic large language model (LLM) could perform computational reproducibility checks at scale. We benchmarked computational reproducibility checks performed by an LLM analyst (Claude Opus running in the Claude Code harness) against results from expert-led reproducibility audits in the social and behavioral sciences and found that LLM accuracy was comparable to that of human experts. Agentic LLMs can now perform high-quality reproducibility checks relatively cheaply, quickly, and easily, putting large-scale audits within reach for journals, granting agencies, organizations, and individual researchers.

articles_hidden.title: How should Moral Motivation be Represented? The Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA)
articles_hidden.authors: Paul McKee; Gregory Russell Samanez-Larkin; Scott A. Huettel; Walter Sinnott-Armstrong
articles_hidden.abstract: Moral psychology has mostly asked which motives drive moral action, and rarely how moral motivation should be represented once several are active at once. Most theories represent it as a single dominant motive or as one continuum from bad to good. Both discard information: a person torn between strong competing motivations and a person who feels nothing occupy the same position. We argue that representational format is a testable empirical claim, not a modeling convenience, and propose the Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA), which represents moral motivation as four independent dimensions formed by crossing motivational direction (approach, avoid) with perceived moral valence (good, bad). MoMA does not specify which motives matter; it specifies the space in which they combine. We derive requirements for an adequate architecture, show that lower-rank representations necessarily collapse psychologically distinct states, and state predictions distinguishing MoMA from simpler alternatives.

articles_hidden.title: Coordinated Psychological Intervention Ensembles Outperform Single-Mechanism Designs Across Societal Challenges
articles_hidden.authors: Anandita Sabherwal; Danielle Goldwert; Madalina Vlasceanu; Elke U. Weber
articles_hidden.abstract: Behavioral science tends to seek the single most predictive explanation for behavioral phenomena and subsequently the most effective intervention for behavior change. Yet many consequential outcomes, from climate action to democratic attitudes, result from multiple psychological processes, raising the question of whether combining interventions that leverage different processes would prove more effective. Across a 13-intervention megastudy and a second, megastudy-informed experiment (Ns = 8,488 and 2,547 US adults; both quota-matched and preregistered) we test whether intervention ensembles—deliberate combinations of distinct psychological modules delivered together—can more effectively shape target behaviors and attitudes.  We test three principles for constructing such ensembles: 1) outcome optimizing ensembles (combining top-performing individual interventions), 2) mechanism coverage ensembles (covering key psychological drivers of the outcome), and 3) multi-level synergy ensembles (combining individual-, collective-, and system-level processes). Ensembles consistently outperformed their constituent single-mechanism interventions. In Study 1, relative to an informed control, the strongest ensemble increased climate policy support by 41.5% and donation by 43.0%. And in Study 2, the ensemble was significantly more effective than its components in reducing partisan animosity and strengthening democratic attitudes. The largest gains were achieved by multi-level synergistic ensembles that aligned processes across individual, collective, and systemic levels. LLM-assisted analyses of participant reasoning reveal that effective ensembles work by resolving complementary psychological barriers, not by simply providing more arguments. For complex societal challenges shaped by multiple barriers, interventions can achieve behavior change at greater rate and scale by designing coordinated intervention ensembles rather than by searching for the single best mechanism.

articles_hidden.title: Legislative Inconsistencies in Defining Psychology Registration in the Criminal Code Act 1899 (Qld): Mandatory Reporting and Implications for Provisional Psychologists
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Paul Sullivan
articles_hidden.abstract: 2021 amendments to the Criminal Code Act 1899 (Qld) in Queensland to criminalise the non-disclosure to police of child sexual abuse (CSA) (s229BC) had consequential implications for the practice of psychology, particularly psychotherapy. Where patients make self-disclosures about current or historical CSA perpetrated against them by an adult when they were a minor (including historical CSA in a now adult patient), psychologists, like all adults in Queensland are required to report that to police, unless one of the “reasonable excuses” against disclosure applies. This paper discusses the wording in the Act with a focus on relevant reasonable excuses in the therapy context, and how the Act contains ambiguity in the application of the law to psychology trainees who are provisional, rather than student registrants under the national health practitioner regulatory scheme.

articles_hidden.title: A decision support toolkit for AI-ready neuroscience data governance
articles_hidden.authors: Wilhelmina M. Botes; Artur Mendes; Bart Huffman; Madison Fleischaker; Ciara Staunton; Beverley Townsend; Paul Ogendi; Lukman Abdulrauf; Andrea Parziale; Gabriela Skoczylas-Kizak
articles_hidden.abstract:
Contemporary human neuroscience relies on exchanging and analyzing neurodata across global institutions and
jurisdictions. However, regulatory architecture fails to maintain continuity of protection across distributed research
environments. Our comparison of 93 countries and 10 operative governance units across Africa, Europe, Latin
America and the Caribbean, and North America shows that neurodata are rarely recognized as distinct regulatory
objects, usually falling under broader legal classifications. While international sharing is permitted in principle,
transformation into derivatives, embeddings, and AI models raises questions about the scope and implementation of
continuing safeguards. We show that international exchange is defined by conditional interoperability, where effective
safeguards require aligning legal, institutional, and technical controls. To operationalize these findings, we introduce a
modular governance toolkit for the data-to-model lifecycle, including a Neurodata Risk Classification Framework,
decision support tools for neurodata transfer and transformation, and a Neurodata Transfer and Access Agreement to
sustain protection without global legal harmonization.

articles_hidden.title: Error correction necessitates immediate, answer-containing feedback: Challenging error suppression, episodic reinstatement, and semantic mediation accounts
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Folger; Matthew Rhodes; Jexy An Nepangue; Hannah Hausman
articles_hidden.abstract: Generating errors during learning benefits subsequent recall, particularly when corrective feedback is presented immediately. Feedback in existing research conflates notification of error commission with provision of the correct target. Across two experiments, we examined the effects of immediate feedback, delayed feedback, and delayed feedback with an immediate “error” warning on cued and error-cued recall. In Experiment 1, warnings did not mitigate the detrimental effect of delayed feedback on cued recall, indicating that optimal pretesting requires immediate, answer-containing feedback. This challenges two hypotheses of errorful learning: that suppressing errors at encoding facilitates error correction (the error-suppression hypothesis), and that error commission promotes context binding which enables episodic reinstatement during feedback and at test (episodic reinstatement hypothesis). Immediate feedback improved cued recall performance but not participants’ ability to recall the accuracy of their initial responses, further contradicting the possibility of episodic reinstatement at test facilitating target recovery. In Experiment 2, delaying feedback improved error-cued recall, undermining mediator-based accounts which assume that errors function as additional retrieval cues, increasing the likelihood of successfully retrieving the target. We propose that error commission increases attention to the target at encoding, strengthening the cue–target retrieval route.

articles_hidden.title: Can Chimpanzees Imagine a Blue Banana?
articles_hidden.authors: Andrey Vyshedskiy
articles_hidden.abstract: Can a chimpanzee that has learned words for colors and objects find a blue pencil among pencils, straws, and Lego pieces in red, green, and blue? This seemingly simple task requires more than recognizing individual words: it requires integrating the meaning of a color adjective with that of a noun to identify an object possessing both properties. Children typically master this ability by 2.3 years. By age 3, they can integrate two modifiers, such as size and color, to follow instructions like “Find a large green straw.” These achievements mark important milestones in the development of language comprehension, allowing children to combine multiple words into a unified mental representation of an object. Chimpanzees, by contrast, can learn hundreds of words referring to objects, colors, and actions. Yet, despite decades of research, they have not been demonstrated to reliably integrate even a color with a noun. In this paper, we propose a simple neurocognitive account of adjective–noun comprehension. We argue that this ability depends on the development of neural connections that allow the prefrontal cortex to modify sensory representations of objects in posterior cortical regions. This framework offers a testable explanation for a fundamental difference between human and chimpanzee language comprehension.

articles_hidden.title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Geller
articles_hidden.abstract:
Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they
address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to
that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a
text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that
every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved
memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same
specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually
long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.
Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,
and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention
selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers
recognize an answer.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring bilingual vocabulary: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Alvin Wei Ming Tan; Federica Moro; Gianmatteo Farabolini
articles_hidden.abstract: Bilingual vocabulary size is often compared with monolingual scores, especially when bilingual normative data are not available, but there is no agreement on how to measure it. Bilingual scores commonly rely on a single language score, on the total amount of words known across languages (total vocabulary) or on the sum of concepts known in either language (conceptual vocabulary). We conducted a Bayesian network meta-analysis comparing these three bilingual measures against monolingual scores, and analyzed the effect of age, vocabulary domain (receptive and expressive), instrument type (direct or parent-report), language development status and language distance. Out of 3747 records retrieved from ERIC, PubMed, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar, we included 226 studies reporting data on 50,020 children. Conceptual vocabulary did not credibly differ from monolingual scores (g = −0.08, 95% CrI [−0.38, 0.21]), whereas total vocabulary was larger and single-language vocabulary smaller. Across age, total vocabulary moved further from monolingual scores and single-language vocabulary moved closer to them, while conceptual vocabulary showed no reliable change. Bilingual-monolingual differences were more negative for expressive than for receptive vocabulary across bilingual measures, and direct tests widened the gap for single-language scores only. Language development status and language distance had no reliable effects, but both were sparsely sampled. When bilingual vocabulary size has to be compared with the monolingual one, conceptual vocabulary is the closest measure. Evidence remains limited beyond the age of six, in clinical populations and for language pairs that do not include English.

articles_hidden.title: Engagement Trajectories in a Jail-Based Dialectical Behavior Therapy Group
articles_hidden.authors: Lindsay Stall; Edelyn Verona
articles_hidden.abstract: Jail-based mental health interventions are delivered under conditions of short and unpredictable stays, making treatment engagement difficult to evaluate. Although Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) has demonstrated promise in correctional settings, little is known about how engagement changes over time in jail-based DBT. Participants (N = 325; 84.9% male) were enrolled in a six-week, jail-adapted DBT skills group as part of a larger randomized controlled trial. Facilitators provided weekly ratings of attendance, in-session participation, homework completion, and diary card completion. Latent Profile Growth Modeling identified engagement trajectories among participants who attended at least three sessions (N = 232), and mixed-effects models examined whether profile membership predicted changes in mental health symptoms and coping. Participants attended an average of approximately 6 of 12 sessions, and 40.2% completed the full cycle. Noncompletion occurred through multiple routes, including release or transfer and the program’s three-miss attendance criterion. Three trajectories were identified: Declining Engagement (37.5%), High-Stable Engagement (29.7%), and High Early Engagement with Drop-Off (32.8%). The High-Stable group had the highest attendance and completion rate. The Declining group showed lower in-session participation, homework completion, and diary card completion beginning early in treatment, whereas the High Early Engagement with Drop-Off group remained relatively engaged across these indicators before a later decline in attendance. Noncompletion in the latter group was primarily associated with release or transfer. Profile membership was not associated with differential changes in symptoms or coping, although mental health symptoms and maladaptive coping decreased overall. These findings show that repeated engagement measures can distinguish early, broad declines in participation from later interruptions in attendance that would be obscured by completion status alone.

articles_hidden.title: Leveraging Consensus-Based Ratings to Assess Dimensions of Early Life Adversity: Links to Emotion Regulation and Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Mark S. Chen; Alexis Brieant; Isabella Kate Kate Peckinpaugh; Leila Adames; Ante Dany; Dylan G. Gee
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Dimensional models of early life adversity (ELA) posit distinct developmental consequences of threat, deprivation, uncontrollability, and unpredictability. Existing approaches force each event into a single dimension or rely on self-ratings that may conflate exposure with subjective appraisal.
Objective: We evaluated consensus-based dimensional ratings as an alternative and examined their associations with emotion regulation and psychopathology.
Participants and Setting: A Prolific sample (N=200; Mage=23.06; 49.5% female; 48% racial minorities) was used to derive the consensus values; a community sample (N=291; Mage=22.40; 59.5% female; 60.5% racial minorities) was used to test their transportability out of sample.
Methods: In Sample 1, we derived consensus values from averaged ratings of 82 ELA items and compared consensus-based and self-rating scoring (feasibility test). In Sample 2, we applied Sample 1 consensus values (transportability test). Dimension scores—threat, deprivation, unpredictability, uncontrollability—predicted cognitive reappraisal, emotion dysregulation, and psychopathology symptoms.
Results: Uncontrollability and unpredictability were highly collinear with threat and deprivation (VIFs > 50) and thus not retained in regression models. Consensus-based scoring was feasible in Sample 1, and consensus-based associations transported to Sample 2. Deprivation was associated with depression, PTSD, and emotion dysregulation in both samples (R² = .04-.22, ps < .01), and negatively with cognitive reappraisal (p = .007).
Conclusions: ELA dimensions are separable at an event level but entangled at the person level, preventing clean specificity in naturalistic samples noted in the literature. Consensus-based values may offer a way to select samples with distinct exposure profiles, treat self–consensus discrepancies as meaningful appraisal differences, and evaluate whether such appraisals could be intervention targets.

articles_hidden.title: Is it Loneliness or Misfit? – Disentangling Predictors of Populist Attitudes and Voting  Intentions
articles_hidden.authors: Alma-Sophia Merscher; Anja S. Göritz; Janosch Schobin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Loneliness has been associated with various so-called "anti-democratic" attitudes and behaviors 
such as populist voting intentions, voting abstention, and populist attitudes. However, several 
other constructs pertaining to feelings of social disconnection conceptually overlap with 
loneliness and have similarly been linked to anti-democratic outcomes. Among those constructs
are perceptions of being a societal misfit—feelings of not fitting in with the cultural 
mainstream—that have been positively associated with voting abstention. Hitherto it was
unclear whether loneliness uniquely explains populist voting intention, voting abstention, and 
populist attitudes, or whether these associations are better accounted for by perceptions of 
societal misfit. In three online studies (ntotal = 3,017), we tested whether loneliness and misfit 
are empirically distinct and whether they uniquely predict these outcomes. Factor analyses 
suggested that loneliness and misfit are related but distinct constructs. Although both constructs 
significantly the measured predicted political outcomes when considered separately in most 
samples, only misfit retained unique predictive power when both were modeled jointly. These 
findings underscore the importance of disentangling related constructs pertaining to perceived 
social disconnection when explaining political outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Speaking through shared hubs, not gendered spokes? Exploring sex-related variation in object naming in Tunisian Arabic-speaking people with post-stroke aphasia
articles_hidden.authors: Amina KLIBI
articles_hidden.abstract: Whether sex-related factors shape confrontational object naming in non-Western clinical populations remains understudied within the Controlled Semantic Cognition framework. We evaluated naming performance across eight semantic categories and three overall measures in 14 native Tunisian Arabic speakers with post-stroke aphasia (6 males, 8 females). Group differences were examined using nonparametric Mann–Whitney U tests and Bayesian analyses. Uncorrected comparisons initially favored female patients in Furniture naming (p = .023) and Total Immediate Responses (p = .043). However, no category-level differences survived correction for multiple comparisons. Bayesian analyses predominantly supported the null hypothesis (BF₀₁ = 1.24–2.15), with Furniture showing only weak, inconclusive evidence for a sex effect (BF₁₀ = 1.93). Overall, results provide no convincing evidence of systematic sex-related disparities in object naming. These findings align with a shared amodal semantic hub rather than gendered spokes, though larger studies are required to confirm sex invariance in this population.

articles_hidden.title: The Approximate Number System is an unlikely account for symbolic number comparison
articles_hidden.authors: Attila Krajcsi
articles_hidden.abstract: The approximate number system (ANS) is an imprecise representation of numbers that is widely assumed to support both symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical tasks. It is believed to be not only the foundation for simple numerical operations but also for higher-level mathematical thinking. One fundamental support for the ANS is the existence of the ratio effect in symbolic number comparison. That is, for example, when Arabic numbers are compared, human performance is proportional to the ratio of the to-be-compared values, similar to psychophysical comparison of perceptual features. A critical issue with this account, however, is that an exact operation, which is required in symbolic number comparison, cannot be backed solely by an imprecise representation. This is for several reasons. First, while a psychophysical model assumes imprecise representation, humans can compare symbolic numbers with arbitrarily high precision. Second, psychophysical models predict worse performance for number pairs with a relatively small ratio than the actual human performance. Third, if an additional mechanism supporting exact comparison is also assumed, current empirical evidence cannot verify the ANS model. Fourth, the ANS account differentiates approximate and exact tasks, where only approximate tasks can be solved purely with the ANS. However, the comparison task is assumed to be processed purely by the ANS, even if the task is exact. Taken together, these arguments make the ANS an unlikely account for symbolic number comparison. While these arguments question the role of the ANS in symbolic number processing, the ANS may have a role in nonsymbolic number processing, although the general relevance of the ANS may be considerably lower than assumed by previous works. Consequently, the individual differences in the sensitivity of the ANS may be less critical in higher-level math performance, dyscalculia diagnosis, or training programs.

articles_hidden.title: The Family Criticism Paradigm: A Laboratory Task for Investigating Psychophysiological Responses in Parent–Child Triads
articles_hidden.authors: Matias M. Pulopulos; Nadischa Helena Dierdorp; Melanie De Leener; Mariah Matar; Michel Sfeir; Sien Verelst; Shiyao Wang; Federico Cassioli; Guy Bosmans; Eva Ceulemans
articles_hidden.abstract: Investigating stress regulation processes within the family context offers important evidence to understand the development of mental and physical health problems. However, laboratory paradigms for investigating stress in several family members simultaneously are limited. The present study introduces and evaluates a standardized paradigm to investigate psychophysiological responses to family-framed standardized evaluative feedback in parents and children simultaneously. A total of 120 families (consisting of a mother, father, and their child aged 10-12 years) participated in a laboratory session in which they were individually but simultaneously exposed to neutral, praising, and critical audio comments presented as originating from the other two family members.
