Psychophysiological response was assessed using mood, state rumination, and autonomic nervous system activity measures, including vagally mediated heart rate variability (HRV), pre-ejection period (PEP), and skin conductance level (SCL). Results showed that criticism increased negative affect (tension, sadness, anger) and decreased positive affect in both parents and children. Self-critical rumination increased 5 and 10 min after the exposure to the paradigm. At the physiological level, HRV was lower during both praise and criticism than during neutral comments, indicating reduced parasympathetic activity during social evaluation. During recovery, HRV increased, suggesting a rebound in parasympathetic activity, while sympathetic responses showed decreased cardiac sympathetic activity (PEP) in parents and increased sympathetic activation (SCL) in children. These findings support the use of this paradigm for eliciting affective, cognitive, and physiological stress responses among family members, offering a promising approach for research on stress regulation and resilience within family systems.

articles_hidden.title: Ambiguity Preferences Are Distinct from Beliefs About Risk
articles_hidden.authors: Syed Farhad Ali Shah; Jeffrey B. Dennison; James B. Wyngaarden; John A. Clithero; David Victor Smith
articles_hidden.abstract: Debates across the behavioral sciences have long examined whether ambiguity avoidance in decision making reflects stable preferences for certainty or uncertainty in beliefs formed through limited experience. Prior studies have commonly used the max–min expected utility (MMEU) model to interpret ambiguity-related decisions, but MMEU confounds preferences with beliefs by focusing on the range of possible probabilities rather than how individuals form them. We conducted two experiments (N = 53; N = 298) using a Linked Colored Lottery Task to test whether ambiguity avoidance reflects stable preferences or beliefs about outcome distributions. Participants first learned to associate colors with distinct outcome distributions by sampling from them and then made incentivized choices between options that varied in ambiguity. This design allowed us to observe how beliefs about distributional variance influenced decisions and to distinguish whether choices reflected belief construction versus uncertainty evaluation. We compared models based on MMEU and on subjective recursive expected utility (SREU), which explicitly separates beliefs from preferences. In both experiments, model comparison favored SREU, and participants with more dispersed inferred beliefs were more likely to avoid ambiguous options. Sampling patterns and memory for probabilities showed similar effects. Apparent age-related differences in ambiguity avoidance were also better explained by belief variance than by preferences. These results suggest that ambiguity avoidance often reflects perceived imprecision in learned beliefs rather than an inherent aversion to uncertainty, plausibly a cognitive rather than affective phenomenon, with implications for understanding decision making across learning, memory, and uncertainty processing domains.

articles_hidden.title: Who Will Conduct Science?  Researchers’ Expectations of AI Capabilities and the Future of Scientific Work
articles_hidden.authors: Balazs Aczel; Dianovics Dominik; Peter Szecsi; Barnabas Szaszi
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI systems have demonstrated their potential to outperform humans in conducting research and in answering previously unsolved scientific problems. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing research independently, the question shifts from how researchers should use AI to how much human resources will be required in scientific research and where. We surveyed researchers worldwide about their perspectives on AI-driven scientific research, prompted by OpenAI’s bulk release of mathematical solutions in October 2026. We received over 4,000 responses from researchers across 126 countries and a wide range of disciplines. Most respondents (62%) expected AI systems to be capable of conducting research tasks independently within three years, although expectations regarding the quality of AI-generated research varied, with 41% anticipating quality comparable to or exceeding that of competent human researchers. Respondents generally supported allowing AI to assume most roles in scientific research (each with a minimum of 48%), mainly under human supervision. AI developments made one-third of respondents concerned about their own job security; mathematicians and statisticians anticipated the greatest effects on their research and careers (45%), and researchers in the humanities and arts the least (30%). Despite concerns about potential negative career consequences, respondents overwhelmingly (74%) expected AI-driven research to accelerate scientific progress. Although the limitations of this survey restrict the generalizability of its findings, the results offer an overview of how researchers across more than a hundred countries perceive rapid advances in AI. They also highlight the need to monitor AI’s impact on the scientific workforce and inform policies that support the sustainable integration of AI into scientific research.

articles_hidden.title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder across the Menstrual Cycle and the Role of Sleep Quality and Perceived Stress
articles_hidden.authors: Sibel Nayman; Janna Del Din; Marlene Bobach Ríos; Lilli Jung; Julia Neutz; Lea Reiter; Stefanie Schäfer; Aylin Yakin; Melda Polat; Nikolaus Kleindienst
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Emerging evidence indicates perimenstrual exacerbation of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in females and reduced perceived stimulant responsiveness during the luteal phase. Prospective studies jointly examining daily ADHD symptoms, medication use, sleep, and perceived stress across the menstrual cycle are lacking.

Aims
(1) To characterize cyclical variation, including latent profiles, in ADHD symptoms, functional impairment, perceived stress, sleep quality, and medication use; (2) to examine whether sleep quality and perceived stress predict next-day symptoms and impairment across the cycle.

Methods
Naturally cycling adult females with ADHD (N=125) completed a digital daily diary across their menstrual cycle. Sleep quality was reported each morning; evening en-tries assessed ADHD symptoms (inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity), functional impairment, perceived stress, and ADHD-specific medication use.

Results
Generalized additive mixed models showed significant perimenstrual increases in ADHD symptoms, impairment, and perceived stress with significant individual heter-ogeneity. Medication was most often taken as usual in the late luteal phase and more often omitted in the follicular phase. Growth mixture models identified sub-groups with mid-luteal or perimenstrual peaks in 16–30% for inattention, impulsivity, and impairment, and in 42–57% for hyperactivity and perceived stress, but not for sleep quality. Lower average sleep quality and higher average perceived stress were associated with greater symptom severity regardless of cycle phase; day-to-day stress increases additionally predicted greater next-day impairment.

Conclusions
A subgroup of females with ADHD may experience luteal-phase symptom exacerba-tion alongside heterogeneous cyclical subtypes, supporting cycle-sensitive diagnos-tics and treatment planning that accounts for individual variation in symptom trajec-tories, sleep, and perceived stress.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring bilingual vocabulary: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Alvin Wei Ming Tan; Federica Moro; Gianmatteo Farabolini
articles_hidden.abstract: Bilingual vocabulary size is often compared with monolingual scores, especially when bilingual normative data are not available, but there is no agreement on how to measure it. Bilingual scores commonly rely on a single language score, on the total amount of words known across languages (total vocabulary) or on the sum of concepts known in either language (conceptual vocabulary). We conducted a Bayesian network meta-analysis comparing these three bilingual measures against monolingual scores, and analyzed the effect of age, vocabulary domain (receptive and expressive), instrument type (direct or parent-report), language development status and language distance. Out of 3747 records retrieved from ERIC, PubMed, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar, we included 226 studies reporting data on 50,020 children. Conceptual vocabulary did not credibly differ from monolingual scores (g = −0.08, 95% CrI [−0.38, 0.21]), whereas total vocabulary was larger and single-language vocabulary smaller. Across age, total vocabulary moved further from monolingual scores and single-language vocabulary moved closer to them, while conceptual vocabulary showed no reliable change. Bilingual-monolingual differences were more negative for expressive than for receptive vocabulary across bilingual measures, and direct tests widened the gap for single-language scores only. Language development status and language distance had no reliable effects, but both were sparsely sampled. When bilingual vocabulary size has to be compared with the monolingual one, conceptual vocabulary is the closest measure. Evidence remains limited beyond the age of six, in clinical populations and for language pairs that do not include English.

articles_hidden.title: Reconstructing Dörner's 2003 PSI island agent: trace-level validation and implementation-dependent behaviour
articles_hidden.authors: Alec Sproten
articles_hidden.abstract: Dörner's PSI theory treats motivation, emotion and cognition as one regulatory system and was implemented as an agent that lives on a simulated island. The aim of this paper is to open that program, version 4.9.1.200 of 2003, to inspection. We report a reconstruction in Python and its validation against the original running under Wine. For one complete reference life of 739 behaviour cycles, the reconstruction reproduces every compared observable: all 109,140 lines of the activity protocol, all 2,802 actions with their ages, all 43 process counters and the end-of-life files, and the first 75,000 random draws agree in value and call site. In eight further lives every observed difference traces back to a single cause, a byte of a heap address that the original reads as part of a direction name; in four of them this byte changed a decision after 310 to 663 cycles. Whether the two programs produce the same distribution of behaviour has therefore not been tested. Tracing each random draw to its source exposed properties that the published description does not contain, among them a rule for background goals that inverts the rule stated in Dörner's book, side effects of the user interface on memory and time, and unguarded pointer accesses that stalled 3 of 100 reconstructed reference lives. Removing these properties together lowered deaths from 11.95 to 9.35 per 1,000 cycles over 97 paired lives. In this world one need, the collection of nucleotides, held control in 99.9 % of the recorded motive decisions.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological essentialism, compression and the structure of concepts
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Gärdenfors; Matias Osta-Vélez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Psychological essentialism is the tendency to view the members of categories as sharing a
hidden essence that explains their observable properties. From a cognitive point of view,
essentialist beliefs depend partly on judgments that several properties of objects ‘hang
together.
’ As a consequence, humans perceive natural kind categories as having stronger
essences than other categories, such as artifact categories. In this paper, we offer a new way to
explain essentialism as the result of a process of dimensionality reduction involved in the
formation of concepts. More specifically, we propose that a small set of principal components
(as understood from Principal Component Analysis) represents patterns of covariation that can
support essentialist beliefs about categories. We show that our approach accounts for several
empirical findings concerning psychological essentialism. We also discuss how to understand
the functional properties in artifact categories, and the connection between generic language
and essentialism from a developmental perspective.

articles_hidden.title: Dan Parker, Linguistic illusions: A case study on agreement attraction. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2025. Pp. xvi + 171.
articles_hidden.authors: Radim Lacina; Utku Turk
articles_hidden.abstract: This is a review of Dan Parker's book 'Linguistic illusions: A case study on agreement attraction' published by Cambridge University Press in 2025. The book gives a comprehensive summary of both the basics of a myriad of illusory phenomena and of agreement attraction in detail. It is a valuable resource for students and researchers alike, especially thanks to the accessible explanations of the leading issues and theories in the field. We critically discuss the book's reported ACT-R modelling, original experiments and its limited engagement with the cross-linguistic study of attraction.

articles_hidden.title: Depressive symptoms are associated with weaker evidence accumulation and greater caution during social decision-making
articles_hidden.authors: Jinil Kim; Yuan-Wei Yao
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression is often characterized by reduced reward sensitivity, slowed responding, and altered social functioning. Prior drift-diffusion modeling studies have linked depression to less efficient accumulation of decision evidence and to greater decision caution in non-social decision-making tasks. However, it remains unclear whether similar process-level alterations extend to social decision-making tasks, such as the ultimatum game, which involves weighing monetary reward against emotional reactions to another player’s offer. To address this question, we applied drift-diffusion models to a publicly available dataset in which 351 adults, grouped by the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), responded to offers in the ultimatum game. Participants with elevated depressive symptoms accepted offers at a rate comparable to those with lower symptoms but responded more slowly. In a standard time-stationary diffusion model, the high depressive-symptom group showed weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, indexed by lower drift rate and wider decision thresholds, respectively. In an exploratory time-varying model that allowed different attributes to enter the decision process at different times, the same group differences in drift rate and decision threshold were observed. Additionally, the difference between reward and emotion information was estimated to enter the decision process later in the high depressive-symptom group. These findings suggest that depression-related slowing during social decision-making may arise from weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, which are not apparent from acceptance rates alone.

articles_hidden.title: Contrast merger in the perception and production of bilingual speakers
articles_hidden.authors: Caihong WENG; Alexander Martin; Martijn Wieling; Ioana CHITORAN
articles_hidden.abstract:
In this study, we examine two Mandarin fricative contrasts that are variably merged in Quanzhou Southern Min–Mandarin bilingual speech. The Mandarin /f/∼/x/ contrast contains a sound /f/ that is absent from Southern Min but that can be assimilated to /hw/, making it distinct from /x/. The Mandarin /s/∼/ʂ/ contrast contains a sound /ʂ/ that is entirely absent from Southern Min and can only be assimilated to /s/. We compare speakers’ perception and production patterns for these two contrasts and and ask whether the two are related at the level of the individual speaker. Results show that /f/∼/x/ was more accurately discriminated and produced than /s/∼/ʂ/. This asymmetry is consistent with the way the two contrasts map onto the Southern Min inventory, with the acoustic and articulatory differences between them, and with the different social meanings they carry. At the individual level, however, the correlation between perceptual and production accuracy was small and below our adopted significance threshold.
The strength of this relationship did not modulated by contrast, vowel context, generation, or Mandarin usage. Perception and production therefore agree at the group level on which contrast is harder, but a speaker who perceives a contrast more accurately is not reliably the speaker who produces it more accurately.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental Differences in How Experiential and Observational Learning Shape Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Maria A. Woitow; Anthony I. Jang; Ben Eppinger; Marcel Brass; Julia M. Rodriguez Buritica
articles_hidden.abstract: Children’s ability to learn and form memories through direct experience and observation increases with age. However, the development of the underlying mechanisms, particularly prediction errors (PEs), through which both learning modes influence memory, remains unclear. Using an incidental memory paradigm, we compared children (8–10 years) and adults (18–30 years) in how reward PEs (RPEs) during experiential and observational reinforcement learning affect episodic memory. Although children showed weaker learning performance, both age groups remembered images better after experiential than after observational learning, and they did not differ in recognition accuracy. However, adults showed greater memory strength and remembered images better when they or another player gambled for rewards, especially when associated with positive RPEs. In contrast, children recognized images better when they rejected gambles, and exploratory analyses linked better memory to larger unsigned RPEs when they accepted gambles. These findings suggest age differences in how one’s own and observed decisions, and potentially associated reward predictions, shape episodic memory.

articles_hidden.title: Are psychedelic users less susceptible to visual illusions? Evidence from the Illusion Game
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique Makowski; Marco Sperduti; Oliver Collins; Lucie Daudé; Joy Zogheib; Ewen Kervadec; Bruno Roméo; Pascale Piolino; Baptiste Fauvel
articles_hidden.abstract: Classic psychedelics are thought to relax prior expectations, which should weaken visual illusions. Evidence is scarce, especially outside the acute state, and error rates, the usual measure of illusion sensitivity, also depend on overall performance. We tested 118 adults, of whom 44 had never used a classic psychedelic, 39 had used one within the last 30 days (the "afterglow" period) and 35 longer ago. They completed the Illusion Game, a response-time task of judging which of two targets is larger while the strength of an illusion (Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer, vertical-horizontal) varies independently of the real difference between them. A hierarchical drift diffusion model was fitted to every choice and response time. Both user groups set wider decision boundaries than naïve participants, gathering more evidence before responding, and made fewer errors. We then computed an index of illusion sensitivity independent of overall accuracy: the effect of illusion strength on performance relative to that of the real difference. This index was 22% lower in users on average, equally in recent and past users, and unrelated to age, language, student status, psychological flexibility, distress or the intensity of the last experience. It correlated moderately across illusions, less than general performance did. Psychedelic users appeared somewhat less sensitive to illusions, as relaxed priors would predict, but the absence of a clear link with use recency limits interpretative confidence and generalizability.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-linguistic regularities in pronominal number neutralisation are not reflected in learning biases: Synchronic, diachronic, and experimental evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Carmen Saldana; Chundra A. Cathcart; Jessica K. Ivani; Balthasar Bickel; Mora Maldonado
articles_hidden.abstract: Although number neutralisation—the loss of singular-plural distinctions—is relatively rare in paradigms of personal pronouns, it is the most common pattern of pronominal syncretism cross-linguistically and exhibits systematic asymmetries across person values. Number distinctions are most frequently neutralised in third person, less so in second person, and least often in first person. While this generalisation has been widely noted, its empirical foundation to date remains relatively weak, and no clear mechanistic explanation has been established for why this typological asymmetry might arise. To address this gap, we investigate whether cross-linguistic patterns of number neutralisation might reflect biases in learning, such that patterns that are easier to learn are more reliably transmitted over time and consequently become more prevalent across languages. We first conduct a large-scale synchronic analysis of pronominal paradigms (1,243 languages), confirming a frequency-based hierarchy (3rd > 2nd > 1st) but challenging its previously assumed implicational nature (1st > 2nd > 3rd; i.e., if in 1st, then in 2nd, and if in 2nd, then in 3rd). A diachronic phylogenetic analysis suggests a tendency towards greater stability of number neutralisation in the order 3rd > 2nd > 1st. Overall, however, it provides limited support for the frequency-based hierarchy and no clear support for the implicational hierarchy. Finally, an artificial language learning experiment testing the learnability of different neutralisation patterns reveals that learners do not mirror typological tendencies: contrary to predictions—and in line with an author-based bias—first-person number neutralisation appears to be most learnable. These findings suggest that the typological evidence for the number neutralisation hierarchy might not be as robust as previously assumed, and that learning biases alone might not straightforwardly explain the typological tendencies. This challenges the link between learning biases and typological distributions, suggesting that pronominal paradigms evolve in a manner that is less constrained by learning biases, and/or that alternative processing and communicative biases may better account for cross-linguistic distributions of pronominal number neutralisation.

articles_hidden.title: Learning Finnish through English: The role of linguistic distance, exposure, and affective factors in L2 grit
articles_hidden.authors: Natalja Ulrich; Nils Jaekel
articles_hidden.abstract: Sustained effort and perseverance are essential for successful language learning, particularly in contexts where learners face linguistically demanding target languages such as Finnish, taught in L2 English. This study examined the role of linguistic background, language exposure, and emotional factors in explaining variation in L2 grit among 82 early-stage learners of Finnish as a foreign language. Participants completed an online survey assessing linguistic background, exposure to Finnish, language learning enjoyment, anxiety, and L2 grit. Hierarchical linear regression analyses showed that greater linguistic distance to English was consistently negatively associated with lower Finnish L2 grit, while linguistic distance to Finnish became a negative predictor after controlling for exposure. The number of previously learned languages was positively associated with L2 grit. Among exposure-related variables, Finnish media use, but not time spent in Finland, was associated with Finnish L2 grit. Language learning enjoyment emerged as a strong positive predictor, whereas anxiety was not. The findings suggest that perseverance in early-stage Finnish learning is shaped not only by the target language itself but also by multilingual experience, instructional language accessibility, and positive emotional engagement.

articles_hidden.title: Selective maintenance of aversive memories as a mechanism of spontaneous recovery of fear
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Berwian; Yongjing Ren; Sashank Pisupti; Jialing Ding; Seohyun Moon; Jamie C. Chiu; Deepta Chandrasekhar; Yael Niv
articles_hidden.abstract:
Return of fear after exposure poses a significant challenge for treatment of anxiety dis-
orders. In this study, we used computational modeling to test competing mechanisms
underlying spontaneous recovery of fear over time. We fit computational models of a
novel theory of spontaneous recovery—selective maintenance of aversive memories—
to behavior from a fear conditioning and extinction task (N=316), and showed that they
uniquely captured spontaneous recovery and quantitatively outperformed alternative
models embodying theories from the literature. The results were supported across mul-
tiple datasets, including a preregistered replication (N=355) and a sample with mental
health symptoms (N=520). The selective maintenance modeling framework addition-
ally offers mechanistic insights into overgeneralization and the development of anxi-
ety. Indeed, in the symptomatic sample we found that symptoms of generalized anxiety
disorder correlated with estimates of overgeneralization in the model. Through simu-
lations, we further demonstrated that insights from our model can explain how targeted
interventions such as retrieval cues and cognitive interventions can prevent the return
of fear. These results highlight selective maintenance of aversive events in memory as
a critical and testable target for improving anxiety treatments and preventing relapse.

articles_hidden.title: Do Scales Semantically Resemble the Sources They Cite? Embedding Analysis of Construct Proliferation in Five Anomy Instruments
articles_hidden.authors: Mateo Belalcazar; Joan Sebastian Diaz Mona; Nelson Molina Valencia; Yenny Otálora
articles_hidden.abstract:
Construct proliferation in psychology is associated with jingle and jangle fallacies that psychometric methods are not designed to detect. Semantic embeddings offer a complementary approach, but existing applications have compared scales within a single level without bringing in the theoretical texts a construct's tradition rests on. This study extends the embedding framework of Wulff and Mata (2025a) to a
cross-level comparison paired with a documentary audit of citation acts. We embedded 43 items from five anomy scales alongside 3,762 propositions extracted from nine source texts at three analytical levels (foundational texts, scale articles, and items), using six embedding models from three architectural families, and we coded every passage in which a scale article cites a theoretical source. Items formed
  thematic clusters that crossed scale boundaries, beyond the expression of a single homogeneous theme per instrument, while retaining within-scale cohesion, and were rarely nearest to the article that introduced them (14%). All five scale articles were semantically nearest to Merton's (1938) text, a pattern identical across models, stable under bootstrap resampling, and not reproduced by two genre-matched control texts. The documentary audit showed that no article adopts Merton's formulation; the two articles that adopt a foundational text both adopt Durkheim's Suicide, which was the nearest foundation for neither of them. This proximity coexists with the absence of any direct adoption of Merton. This extension, combining semantic proximity with documented citation acts, offers an approach for examining whether the sources an instrument cites are also the ones its content most resembles.

articles_hidden.title: The CEOs Who Won't Be Measured: Access, Self-Other Gaps and Working Hours in a Preregistered CEO-Team Study
articles_hidden.authors: Bill Gallagher
articles_hidden.abstract: Asking a CEO's team to rate the CEO is the most direct way to test how long working hours relate to leadership, and it is the step many CEOs decline. In a preregistered study, invitations reaching an estimated 60,000 or more people produced 90 CEO responses; 49 eligible CEOs of firms with 10 or more people completed a 24-hour time grid and a 12-item Leadership Behavior Inventory. Only 15 produced the three or more team ratings the design required, against a target of 300. First, access was the binding constraint: 43% of eligible CEOs did not hand over a usable team list, those who withheld reported about eight more weekly hours (p = .09), and none of the 10 CEOs above 58 hours reached the analysis. Second, CEOs ordered their strengths and weaknesses much as their teams did (median rank correlation .60) but rated themselves higher on three of four behaviors (composite +0.28 on a 5-point scale, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.59]). An apparent concentration of that gap on weaknesses did not survive a split-half check for regression to the mean, and the preregistered compression test for minimization could not have detected it. Third, team-rated effectiveness declined with CEO hours across the observed 30- to 58-hour range (p = .037), with no detectable threshold, though the result is fragile to single clusters. With a small sample of mostly small and mid-sized firms, likely tilted toward CEOs open to feedback, these are signals, not confirmed effects. I set out the design changes needed to test them.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Sampling in Social Judgment: Examining Variability in Judgments for the Self, Close, and Distant Others
articles_hidden.authors: Tingyue Li; Derek Powell
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing number of theories explain various aspects of cognition through processes of mental "sampling." Under these theories, judgments (e.g. predicting whether a friend will be late) are accomplished by generating and aggregating samples, through simulation or memory retrieval. Here, we examined a key prediction of these theories: that the variability of judgments will be lower when more samples can be drawn. We test this with a novel intervention in a simple social inference task, examining people's ability to judge the probability of various everyday behaviors, comparing judgments made for themselves versus others. Responses were more consistent when predicting their own behavior than that of an acquaintance, suggesting a greater number of samples could be drawn. Surprisingly, we found only a weak relationship between the time spent with a target and the variability of estimates, suggesting that sampling processes may not rely only on retrieval from memory.

articles_hidden.title: Anhedonia and Emotional Processing of Past- and Future-Directed Mental Representations: Behavioral and Event-Related Potential Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Kai Härpfer; Hannes Per Carsten; Anja Riesel; Julia Klawohn; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles_hidden.abstract: Anhedonia may involve difficulties generating affective value from remembered and imagined positive experiences rather than a generalized reduction in immediate pleasure. However, its association with emotional processing across direct stimulus exposure, memory retrieval, and prospection, including the role of negative affect, remain unclear. This preregistered study examined neural and subjective emotional responses in 48 nonclinical adults with varying levels of anhedonia. Participants viewed positive, negative, and neutral images, recalled them, and imagined future experiences involving their content. During 4,000-ms trials, late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes were assessed from 400 to 4,000 ms, alongside subjective affect and imagery vividness ratings. Anhedonia was assessed using the Snaith–Hamilton Pleasure Scale. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between anhedonia and LPP amplitudes across valence conditions and time windows, as well as subjective ratings across valence conditions. During recall, higher anhedonia was associated with reduced positive–neutral LPP differentiation at 1,000–2,000 and 2,000–3,000 ms, alongside lower pleasantness ratings for positive memories. Valence-dependent LPP associations were not significant during encoding or prospection. These findings suggest that altered affective processing of positive memories may be relevant to anhedonia, alongside broader differences in emotional responding and the vividness of mental representations.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Initial Validation of a Brief, Transdiagnostic Measure of Conflict Resolution Difficulties and Ineffective Relational Strategies
articles_hidden.authors: Kasey Stanton; Nicholas J. Brewster; Kayla Michelle Brown; Helena Towne; Jack D Burke; Isabella Whitesides; Christina G McDonnell; Corinne Carlton; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Considerable research in recent decades has focused on developing measures assessing transdiagnostic dimensions, including measures that target dimensional symptoms rather than traditional diagnostic categories. Furthermore, a sizeable literature has focused on assessing social-cognitive vulnerabilities (e.g., experiential avoidance) thought to be linked to an array of symptoms and functioning difficulties, and a range of measures of transdiagnostic, social-cognitive vulnerabilities have been developed. However, few of them include item content directly assessing conflict resolution difficulties and ineffective interpersonal relational strategies, which also are linked to a range of psychopathology and are targeted in cognitive-behavioral and third-wave treatments. We address this gap in the transdiagnostic assessment literature by presenting initial validation data for a measure of ineffective interpersonal strategies across three studies and four samples of participants (N = 301 adults; N = 808 adults self-identifying a mental health diagnosis; N = 368 undergraduate students; N = 226 community adults). Analyses based on these samples spanned evaluation of participant perspectives on item face validity, quantitative examinations of internal structure, test-retest stability, and evaluating validity associations with a range of self-report and interview measures. Results collectively support the initial validation of an efficient interpersonal measure, the 6-item Transdiagnostic Ineffective Relational Strategies Scale (TIRSS), which is provided in appendix materials for free use for research purposes. We discuss future validation steps to build from this work, as well as ideas for sharpening interpersonal and transdiagnostic assessment research more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: The Phenomenology of Non-Ordinary Experiences during Spiritualist Séances
articles_hidden.authors: Everton de Oliveira Maraldi; Ricardo de Oliveira Souza; Juliana Almeida; Ronald Fischer; Maria Eduarda Ismerio Moreira de Oliveira; Vitor de Oliveira Moura da Silva; Luiz Augusto de Queiroz; Amanda Sales Cafezeiro; Marina Saraiva-Mendes; Tiago Bortolini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Non-Ordinary experiences (NOEs), such as feelings of unity with God, hearing voices, and sensing the presence of deceased persons, are prevalent in the general population. They may be life-transforming but are also associated with pathological conditions such as psychosis and dissociation. However, little is known about how cultural appraisals and religious practices shape their phenomenology and psychological impact in non-clinical populations. For the most part, their socio-cognitive and emotional features remain unexplored. The purpose of this study was threefold. Firstly, to investigate the phenomenological characteristics and types of NOEs reported by self-defined spirit mediums from a spiritualist home circle in the city of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Secondly, to explore the role of social context in interpreting and shaping NOEs. Finally, to gain a better understanding of the phenomenological similarities and distinctions of experiences reported in spiritualist contexts with psychopathological constructs such as dissociative and psychotic symptoms. The study used a mixed-methods approach, combining ethnographic observations of spiritualist séances, thematic content analysis of reports of séance-related NOEs, and standardized scales assessing dissociation, absorption, psychotic symptoms, symptoms of common mental disorders, and satisfaction with life. We analyzed a total of 151 independent reports of NOEs provided by a group of mediumship practitioners participating in regular séances over a period of one year and five months. The reports tapped a variety of experiences including intense emotional states (e.g., happiness, gratitude), alterations in consciousness (e.g., feelings of spacing out), spontaneous mental imagery (e.g., visions of the spiritual world), sensory-perceptual experiences (e.g., hearing voices or other unusual sounds), somatic manifestations (e.g., body tremors), and unusual experiences involving the séance table (e.g., vibrations). The experiences reported were episodic, controllable, and restricted to the séances. Overall, they were described as pleasant or innocuous. Mediums generally reported perceiving their lives as satisfying and meaningful and scored similarly to the general population on items indicative of common mental disorders. Given their cultural impact and predominantly positive effects, these experiences bear implications for differential diagnosis, and the role of cultural and religious factors in mental health, wellbeing, and cognition. The spiritualist séance provide a natural environment for observational and experimental studies of intentionally induced non-ordinary states of consciousness.
Keywords: non-ordinary experiences, dissociative experiences, psychotic experiences, psychosis continuum, spirit mediumship, religious rituals, spirituality

articles_hidden.title: Music-Based Interventions for  Cognition and Brain Health: the ARM framework
articles_hidden.authors: Psyche Loui; Jonathan E. Peelle; Jessica Adrienne Grahn
articles_hidden.abstract: Music-based interventions (MBIs) have shown promise in addressing cognitive, motor, and language impairments across neurological and neurodevelopmental conditions. Despite an increasing number of controlled studies that have assessed the potential rehabilitative effects of music, neural mechanisms underlying therapeutic benefits remain poorly understood. Here we present the ARM framework: a neurobiologically-informed model integrating three key systems: Auditory processing networks that encode temporal and spectral features; Reward circuitry activated by musical pleasure and prediction, and Motor systems engaged through auditory-motor coupling and rhythmic entrainment. We examine how specific MBIs leverage these systems to varying degrees and show how understanding these mechanisms is essential for predicting individual treatment response, personalizing interventions, and developing next-generation therapeutic approaches that optimize engagement of specific neural systems.

articles_hidden.title: The Neural Basis of Consciousness During Evening Naps Measured by MEG: A Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Chikayo Hemmi; Angus Leung; Jennifer Windt; Yuki Motomura; Hiroshige Takeichi; Mochine Ishii; Takashi Tsutsumi; Yuri Kawabata; Naoko Takahashi; Shota Hosogai
articles_hidden.abstract: Dream experiences during sleep provide an excellent opportunity to investigate the neural basis of consciousness. Previous studies have examined the neural correlates of dreaming using electroencephalography (EEG), focusing on spectral power in specific frequency bands. However, findings have been inconsistent, particularly regarding the spatiotemporal characteristics of these correlates, raising questions about whether spectral power in specific brain regions and frequency bands reliably reflects dreaming. In this study, we investigate whether neural correlates reported in a highly influential EEG study generalize to consciousness during evening naps, measured using magnetoencephalography (MEG), which offers more accurate source reconstruction than EEG. In Stage 1, the data acquisition team completed data collection, obtaining MEG data and subjective reports using a targeted serial-awakening paradigm. We test the hypotheses that low-frequency neural power is lower, whereas high-frequency neural power is higher during conscious experiences in frontal and posterior regions. We defined data inclusion and exclusion criteria and established pre-specified analytical procedures based on data from two participants. The pilot results from one participant showed a tendency in the hypothesized direction for low-frequency power across regions, whereas no such tendency was observed for high-frequency power. The results from the other participant did not provide sufficient evidence for any of the hypotheses. In Stage 2, an independent analysis team will conduct group-level hypothesis testing according to the pre-specified procedure, using data from the remaining unanalyzed participants (N = 10) who meet the inclusion criteria.

articles_hidden.title: Examining associations between brain volume and alexithymia in autistic youth and young adults
articles_hidden.authors: Goldie McQuaid; Gregory Wallace; Alex Job Said; Stefen Beeler-Duden; Zachary Jacokes; Kevin Pelphrey; Allison Jack
articles_hidden.abstract:
Alexithymia is a dimensional trait including challenges labeling emotions. Alexithymia is elevated in autistic individuals relative to the general population and is suggested to be part of the broader autism phenotype. Alexithymia is also independently associated with emotion regulation challenges, which are more prevalent among autistic persons, and with two of the most common co-occurring conditions among autistic people: depression and anxiety. A better understanding of alexithymia, including its neural correlates, therefore promises to advance our understanding of risk profiles for mental health problems in autistic people.

We therefore sought to: 1) characterize alexithymia in autistic (n=54) and neurotypical (n=56) adolescents and young adults (15-25y) including group and sex differences; 2) examine group and sex differences in brain volume in eight regions of interest implicated in alexithymia; and 3) explore potential interactions between group and brain volume as predictors of alexithymia.

Autistic individuals self-reported significantly higher levels of alexithymia relative to neurotypical individuals, with autistic females reporting the highest levels and neurotypical males the lowest levels. There were no differences in group or sex based on brain volume. Exploratory models predicting alexithymia found a significant interaction between group and right dorsal anterior cingulate cortex volume.

articles_hidden.title: Seeing Through the Lens: Divergent Thinking and the Evaluation of Creative Product Designs
articles_hidden.authors: Vania Ardelia; Maryam Shahbazi; Moritz Reis; Ahmed Moustafa; Radwa Khalil
articles_hidden.abstract: Evaluations of creative products reflect both product characteristics and evaluator attributes. It remains unclear whether the ability to generate original ideas shapes how people evaluate creative products made by others. In this preregistered study, 97 university students first completed the Gough Creative Personality Scale, the openness items of the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and a self-report item on cultural orientation. In random order, they then rated five iconic chair designs on the Creative Product Semantic Scale and completed an Alternative Uses Task with six everyday objects. The chair ratings yielded each chair's perceived originality and perceived functional quality, and a large language model scored the originality of the Alternative Uses Task responses. Divergent-thinking originality did not predict the evaluation of any chair after correction for multiple comparisons, and creative personality did not strengthen this association as predicted. Openness to experience was associated with more favorable ratings of all chairs, whereas cultural orientation, gender, hobbies, and study year were not. In exploratory analyses, the association between perceived originality and perceived functional quality varied across the five chairs. It was strongest for chairs of intermediate perceived originality, a pattern consistent with the most-advanced-yet-acceptable principle. Design features were not manipulated, so this pattern requires confirmation with larger, systematically varied sets of products. Overall, originality in idea generation was not associated with more favorable evaluations of creative products. Evaluator openness and the specific design were more closely related to these judgments.

articles_hidden.title: Differences in associative change between cues trained in compound are better explained by individual prediction errors than by relative certainty
articles_hidden.authors: Amin Jahani; Metin Üngör
articles_hidden.abstract: The present experiments investigated associative changes during compound training involving cues with different learning histories. In six human predictive-learning experiments using the compound-test procedure (Rescorla, 2000), participants learned about the effects of foods (cues) on inflammation (outcome) in a hypothetical patient. Each food could cause decreases in inflammation, increases in inflammation, or had no effect. Cues A and C were trained as excitatory, whereas cues B and D were trained to acquire inhibitory properties. Participants then received compound training in which A and B were presented together and followed by an outcome that should produce associative loss, followed by a final test in which outcome expectations were assessed for the test compounds AD and BC. The initial training designs were expected to produce greater relative certainty about A than B, with A generating a larger individual prediction error than B during the compound training. If cues generating larger individual prediction errors undergo greater associative change, AD should receive lower ratings than BC. Alternatively, if participants preferentially attribute the compound outcome to the less certain cue (theory protection), BC should receive lower ratings than AD. Overall, the compound-test results were more consistent with an individual prediction-error account: AD was rated lower than BC in Experiments 1, 2, 5, and 6. Experiment 3 showed the opposite pattern, consistent with theory protection, but this pattern was not replicated in Experiment 4. We discuss the implications of these findings for the roles of prediction error and certainty in associative learning.

articles_hidden.title: A Dyadic Perspective on Reactive Aggression: Temporal Behavioral and Neural Dynamics in Sibling Interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Koch; Lucia Hernandez-Pena; Dorothea M.G. König; Julia Schräder; Katja Bertsch; Andreas Meyer-Lindenberg; Edward S. Brodkin; Ute Habel; Rik Sijben; Lisa Wagels
articles_hidden.abstract: Aggression contributes to interpersonal conflict and societal harm. Although aggressive behavior unfolds within social interactions, it has largely been studied as an individual process. Siblings offer dyadic contexts in which aggression is shaped by developmental and relational dynamics. Here, we investigated how aggressive behavior and its neural correlates unfold dynamically within and across healthy adult siblings. Ninety-four siblings from 47 dyads completed an interactive version of the Taylor Aggression Paradigm (iTAP) during simultaneous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). We applied actor-partner interdependence models to predict each sibling’s neural activity during aggressive decision-making from both siblings’ neural responses during the preceding provocation feedback phase and tested whether these associations depended on relationship engagement, as measured by the Sibling Type Questionnaire (STQ) Mutuality subscale. Behaviorally, individuals’ subsequent responses were predicted by their own and their sibling’s preceding behavior. In parallel, greater ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) activity during provocation feedback was associated with greater subsequent amygdala activity during aggressive decision-making within and across siblings, whereas lower dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) activity in one sibling was associated with greater subsequent amygdala activity in the other. Relationship engagement strengthened the actor vmPFC-amygdala association and moderated the partner vmPFC-amygdala association. Exploratory analyses linked dmPFC activity during provocation to participants’ previous aggressive decisions, but not subsequent aggression. Together, these findings show that aggression is embedded in temporally structured behavioral and neural dynamics involving both interaction partners, implicating medial prefrontal regulatory systems in dyadic interaction and highlighting the importance of interpersonal reciprocity and relationship history for understanding aggression.

articles_hidden.title: The State of Play: Methodological Reflections on Phenomenological Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Jodie Louise Russell; Lucienne Spencer; Matthew Broome
articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, we reflect on the position of the researcher within the field of phenomenological psychopathology and the ways they can overcome privilege and outsider status in order to more accurately and ethically grasp the structure of disorder experience from the perspective of the person living it. §1 discusses problems incorporating lived experience as well as its challenges within phenomenological psychopathology. §2 introduces the phenomenological notion of play in the work of Husserl and Fink. §3 elaborates on the political and ethical dimensions of play using the work of Lugones, and §4 then discusses how playfulness might be applied in health research to overcome the problems outlined in §1. §5 then gives examples of how play might be utilised within the methodology of phenomenological psychopathology. Overall, we suggest that both researchers and those with lived experience can engage in processes of understanding that can facilitate safe and inclusive interactions through the medium of play.

articles_hidden.title: Pupil Dynamics Track Preparatory Control and Selective Learning in Decision Making
articles_hidden.authors: Yifei Deng; Jonathon R. Howlett; Marcelo G Mattar
articles_hidden.abstract: A unifying theory of phasic pupil responses suggests that pupil diameter reflects information gain following an observation. However, it remains unclear whether pupil responses track information indiscriminately or selectively encode specific types of information, and whether this selectivity shifts across task phases. To address this, we developed a decision making task with information streams from three sources: control signals, decision-relevant stimuli, and decision-irrelevant stimuli. This design allowed us to dissociate pupillary responses to different forms of information gain (Shannon surprise and learning) across sources and phases. Analyzing pupillometry data from 30 participants, we found modulators of pupil responses shifted from perceptual surprise to policy-related learning over the course of trials. Furthermore, cue-related surprise drove responses immediately after its presentation and during perceptual processing of stimuli, whereas decision-relevant learning modulated responses only post-decision. These findings refine the information-theoretic framework by distinguishing automatic, surprise-related dilation from selective, learning-related dilation gated by decision relevance.

articles_hidden.title: Born on Rhythms: Mother–Foetus and -Infant Neurophysiology as a Dynamic System of Metastable Coupled Oscillators
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Ciaunica; Earl K. Miller; Shir Atzil; Antonio Criscuolo
articles_hidden.abstract: The human embryo grows within a pulsatile maternal milieu structured by cardiac, respiratory, locomotor, vocal and circadian rhythms. Here we integrate evidence from embryology, foetal physiology, developmental cognitive neuroscience and chronobiology: we review how the foetal heart and placenta co-develop under maternal haemodynamic forcing, how maternal rhythms reach the foetus and how they may modulate foetal physiology. We propose that multimodal, semi-periodic input streams may provide a temporal reference frame scaffolding early timing abilities and autonomic self-regulation. In this view, we discuss that co-regulation may ground interoception and allostasis. Next, we formalize the mother–foetus and mother-infant dyads as multiscale systems of coupled oscillators spanning about seven orders of magnitude in frequency - from circadian cycles to neural oscillations. Within this coordination-dynamics framework we propose that healthy co-regulation is marked by metastability: flexible and transient coordination, preserving the endogenous tendencies for systems to display endogenous behaviours and to couple with other systems in an adaptive manner. The framework yields testable predictions on the link between dyadic coordination dynamics and developmental outcome. We are, quite literally, born on rhythms.

articles_hidden.title: Gender comes first: Experimental evidence for the representation of gender closer to the noun stem than number across linguistic populations
articles_hidden.authors: Carmen Saldana; Patrick Njue Kanampiu; Jennifer Culbertson
articles_hidden.abstract: Morphosyntactic expression exhibits significant cross-linguistic variation, yet systematic tendencies emerge. Gender and number features are frequently co-expressed within a single exponent, and when realised separately, gender morphology tends to surface closer to the stem. Competing theoretical accounts of gender and number seek to explain these tendencies, but empirical validation remains challenging due to sparse typological data. Across a series of artificial language learning experiments, we demonstrate that learners exhibit a robust preference for placing nominal morphology encoding gender information closest to the stem. This bias, consistent across English, Italian, and Kîîtharaka speakers, holds both for prefixing and suffixing morphology, and across different types of gender and number systems.These results provide a new source of empirical support for theories proposing a gender-first derivation and highlights cognitive constraints influencing morpheme order.

articles_hidden.title: Do Scales Semantically Resemble the Sources They Cite? Embedding Analysis of Construct Proliferation in Five Anomy Instruments
articles_hidden.authors: Mateo Belalcazar; Joan Sebastian Diaz Mona; Nelson Molina Valencia; Yenny Otálora
articles_hidden.abstract:
Construct proliferation in psychology is associated with jingle and jangle fallacies that psychometric methods are not designed to detect. Semantic embeddings offer a complementary approach, but existing applications have compared scales within a single level without bringing in the theoretical texts a construct's tradition rests on. This study extends the embedding framework of Wulff and Mata (2025a) to a
cross-level comparison paired with a documentary audit of citation acts. We embedded 43 items from five anomy scales alongside 3,762 propositions extracted from nine source texts at three analytical levels (foundational texts, scale articles, and items), using six embedding models from three architectural families, and we coded every passage in which a scale article cites a theoretical source. Items formed
  thematic clusters that crossed scale boundaries, beyond the expression of a single homogeneous theme per instrument, while retaining within-scale cohesion, and were rarely nearest to the article that introduced them (14%). All five scale articles were semantically nearest to Merton's (1938) text, a pattern identical across models, stable under bootstrap resampling, and not reproduced by two genre-matched control texts. The documentary audit showed that no article adopts Merton's formulation; the two articles that adopt a foundational text both adopt Durkheim's Suicide, which was the nearest foundation for neither of them. This proximity coexists with the absence of any direct adoption of Merton. This extension, combining semantic proximity with documented citation acts, offers an approach for examining whether the sources an instrument cites are also the ones its content most resembles.

articles_hidden.title: Motivational Framing Shapes Effort Judgments in Individuals with Depressive Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas Meyer; Rebecca Kochtokrax; Hannah Sautmann; Nexhmedin Morina
articles_hidden.abstract: Effort-related motivational deficits in depression are often studied through effort-reward decisions, yet everyday effort also depends on the reference standards against which it is judged. In a preregistered laboratory crossover study, 51 participants with at least mild depressive symptoms received two opposing effort framings: self-initiated allocation toward goals and need frustration emphasizing burden and affective demand. After reconstructing previous-day activities, participants evaluated upward and downward social, temporal-past, criteria-based, and counterfactual standards for their two most effortful activities per session, yielding 1,632 standard-endorsement judgments followed by intensity and discrepancy ratings for endorsed standards. As predicted, need-frustration framing increased endorsement of upward criteria-based standards (“this should feel less effortful”). However, this effect did not generalize across upward comparisons. Instead, need frustration decreased upward temporal standards (“this used to feel easier”) and increased downward counterfactual standards (“it could have been harder under worse circumstances”). Intensity ratings among endorsed standards were not reliably affected, although an exploratory relevance score supported the specific role of upward criteria-based standards. Perceived effort was higher under allocation but correlated more positively with depressive symptoms under need frustration. These findings suggest that motivational framing changes the comparison standards people identify as relevant to everyday effort judgments and highlight the need to assess the appraised meaning of effort-related comparisons directly.

articles_hidden.title: Researching Traditionally Rooted Psychological Concepts: Methodological Implications from Traditional Chinese Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Xianglong ZENG
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on psychological concepts rooted in historical intellectual traditions has attracted growing attention, yet studies in this field may investigate fundamentally different psychological objects. The present article conceptualizes the modern and traditional approaches to such research and systematically examines their methodological implications. Whereas the modern approach constitutes its objects primarily through contemporary manifestations within a population, the traditional approach specifies psychological targets through theoretical formulations grounded in classical accounts. Such targets may have theoretically specified internal relations and need not already be realized in the populations available for research. Drawing on existing studies of traditional Chinese psychology, the analysis identifies potential methodological mismatches and demonstrates their implications for empirical investigation. Ordinary participants may not possess the understanding or degree of realization required to investigate a target mentality; cultivation may be a methodological precondition rather than merely an intervention to modify existing tendencies; and satisfactory psychometric results do not necessarily establish that a measure represents the target’s intended meanings and internal relations. Moreover, findings from partial realizations cannot simply be generalized to fully cultivated forms. These analyses provide principles for selecting participants, determining the role of intervention, evaluating measurement, and delimiting the scope of inference according to the intended research object and question. The article also considers how empirical evidence can inform the evaluation and possible revision of classical psychological claims, while distinguishing empirical investigation from the normative justification of cultivation. Beyond traditional psychology, these methodological insights may inform empirical research on psychological possibilities specified through other theoretical sources.

articles_hidden.title: Language at Scale: Functional Informational Interchangeability and the Child–LLM Data Gap
articles_hidden.authors: Yonata Levy
articles_hidden.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable linguistic competence through exposure to
far more language than children ever encounter. We examine whether this Child–LLM data gap
rests on an incomplete comparison of the information available to children. Drawing on language
acquisition research and information theory, we propose Functional Informational
Interchangeability: extensive linguistic input can supply models with information that is
interchangeable with the information children obtain through combined linguistic, perceptual,
motor, emotional and social experiences. Relevance, redundancy, joint information and learnerdependent uptake provide tools for testing this hypothesis. The proposal reframes the Child–
LLM data gap around information relevant to acquiring linguistic knowledge. If the
contributions of these environments prove comparable in task-relevant informational units, the
apparent gap may disappear.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable prospective effects between workplace incivility and depressive and anxious mood: A reassessment of Cao et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Cao et al. reported longitudinal associations between workplace incivility and depressive and anxious mood based on cross-lagged panel analyses. However, the detection of statistically significant cross-lagged coefficients does not necessarily demonstrate the existence of underlying prospective effects because comparable patterns can emerge under alternative data-generating mechanisms. In the present study, we recreated the sample size and correlational structure reported by Cao et al. using simulated data and evaluated the robustness of the findings across several analytically defensible model specifications. The estimated effects varied markedly across approaches. Whereas some models yielded positive prospective associations, others produced negative or statistically nonsignificant estimates. When the results from all specifications were synthesized using meta-analytic techniques, none of the aggregated effects differed significantly from zero. These findings suggest that available evidence does not provide a strong basis for claims about prospective relationships between workplace incivility and depressive or anxious mood. In line with recommendations from the multiverse-analysis literature, inferences should be guided by the extent to which results replicate across reasonable analytical decisions rather than by a single modeling strategy.

articles_hidden.title: Stage 1 Registered Report: Levels and Types of Processing: Levels of Processing for Recall of Color-Object Associations After Perceptual Encoding Tasks
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Rihs; Nicolas Rothen
articles_hidden.abstract: According to the levels of processing account, memory recall improves when information is encoded at a deep rather than at a shallow level of processing. Most studies demonstrated this levels of processing effect by comparing a perceptual with a semantic type of processing for verbal material. While some studies have also demonstrated levels of processing effects using only semantic types of processing, it remains unclear whether such effects can also occur using only perceptual types of processing. The current study aims at showing a levels of processing effect for color-object associations after a perceptual type of processing. In a new orientation task, participants are asked to compare images either on a shallow (“Is the image larger than the reference image?”) or on a deep level of processing (“Does the image differ from the reference image?”). In Experiment 1, we will replicate previous findings on the processing effect in image-color associations using concrete objects within the new task framework. In Experiment 2, we will extend these findings to abstract stimuli, thereby testing the generalizability of the effect beyond semantically meaningful content. Participants are expected to show improved recall of color-image associations when they are processed on a deep rather than on a shallow level. Overall, the current study should give further insights into levels of processing theory by showing that a processing effect occurs without the involvement of semantic processing.

articles_hidden.title: Distinguishing ingroup and outgroup germ aversion improves prediction of intergroup attitudes during the COVID-19 pandemic
articles_hidden.authors: Jeana Kataria; Brian O'Shea
articles_hidden.abstract: During infectious disease outbreaks, contamination concerns can become attached to social groups. Existing germ-aversion measures rarely specify the perceived source of contamination. Using data collected during the first U.S. peak of COVID-19, we tested whether target-specific germ aversion (ingroups/local region versus outgroups/developing countries) improves the prediction of intergroup attitudes during the COVID-19 pandemic, reflecting the possibility that unfamiliar outgroups are perceived as greater sources of novel pathogens. Across explicit (e.g., perceived health and warmth; Ns = 1,450–1,460) and implicit (Brief Implicit Association Test; Ns = 378–1,311) attitudes targeting ingroups (US, White People) and outgroups (China, Italy, UK, Asian, Brown and Black People), we find that outgroup—but not ingroup or general—germ aversion was the most consistent predictor of ingroup preference and outgroup derogation, even after controlling for infectability and COVID-19 concern. These results suggest that contamination concerns linked to foreign or developing-country contexts can provide modest incremental information about intergroup attitudes during a politicised public-health crisis, highlighting the value of specifying the targets and contexts of pathogen concern when applying disease-avoidance psychology to intergroup questions.

articles_hidden.title: The Environmental Includes the Social: On the Psychological Structure of Altruistic and Biospheric Values
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Eric Neef; Quinn J Hundgen; Siegmar Otto; P. Wesley Schultz
articles_hidden.abstract: Ample research discusses the relationship between altruistic (human-oriented) and biospheric (nature-oriented) values. Some propose a single, other-oriented construct. Others argue for two related but distinct constructs. Extending the Inclusion Model of Environmental Concern, we propose a third position: biospheric values include altruistic values. Across three studies spanning 53 countries (Study 1: N = 222, U.S. sample; Study 2: N = 791, U.S. sample; Study 3: N = 85,796, 52 countries), we find support for this inclusion model. First, across much of the world, individuals who hold strong biospheric values also tend to hold strong altruistic values, whereas holding strong altruistic values does not imply holding strong biospheric values to the same extent. Second, biospheric and altruistic values predicted humanitarian outcomes similarly, but biospheric values predicted environmental outcomes better than altruistic values. Third, a bifactor-(S-1) model representing the Inclusion Model fit the data better than two alternatives, a unidimensional model or a correlated two-factor model. Finally, we demonstrate how modeling data in line with the Inclusion Model resolves interpretational challenges that can arise when treating both values as unidimensional (i.e., lack of discrimination) or correlated (e.g., suppression). The inclusion model advances theoretical understanding of biospheric and altruistic values. Effects commonly attributed to biospheric values may partly reflect their altruistic core. Practically, interventions targeting biospheric values may also tap into altruistic values, whereas interventions appealing to altruistic values can reach broader audiences. Future work should determine the model’s boundaries and explore global heterogeneity.

articles_hidden.title: The role of neuroscience for psychological causal explanation
articles_hidden.authors: Beate Krickel; Markus Werkle-Bergner
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology provides causal explanations of behavior but it remains contested whether such explanations are scientifically legitimate without grounding in neuroscience. Two prominent arguments have been put forward to argue for the dependence of psychology on neuroscience: first, the classical causal exclusion argument argues that higher-level causes are excluded by lower-level causes. Second, according to a more recent argument, psychological models only provide how-possibly explanations but not how-actually explanations unless the variables and relations they postulate correspond to underlying neural mechanisms. In this article, we defend the independence of psychological causal explanation. Based on an interventionist account of causation, we argue that a psychological model is causally explanatory when it identifies variables that serve as points of intervention. Still, we show that neuroscience sometimes has a crucial role for validating psychological models: when a psychological model identifies points of interventions that cannot be intervened on at the psychological level.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic resource allocation in temporal working memory: interplay of decay, interference and attention
articles_hidden.authors: Yunyun Shen; Sophie K Herbst; Virginie van Wassenhove
articles_hidden.abstract: How does a moment become a memory trace? The transition from perceived duration to the when of memory is likely shaped by attention and working memory (WM). In two experiments, we investigated how memory decay, interference between stored durations, and internal versus external attention affect the precision of recall from temporal WM. For this, we used a delayed reproduction task in which participants listened to a sequence of time intervals and reproduced them after a retention period (Herbst et al., 2025). In Experiment 1, we manipulated the ratio between the target interval and the retention interval, showing that both the duration of the retention interval (decay) and its ratio to the target (temporal distinctiveness yielding interference) affected WM performance. In Experiment 2, we examined interference between intervals within a sequence by manipulating attention via a cue indicating which interval to reproduce. The cue appeared either before (pro-cue) or after (retro-cue) the retention period, directing external attention to sensory encoding or internal attention to WM representations, respectively, either for a single item or the full sequence. External attention selectively benefited accuracy and precision for the longest item when cued alone in the final position. Retro-cueing, by contrast, more generally reduced precision for single-item compared to the whole-sequence recall. Finally, a mixture modeling approach revealed swap errors consistent with those observed in visual WM. Together, these findings compare the contributions of decay and temporal distinctiveness to temporal WM performance with a dynamic resource allocation framework.

articles_hidden.title: Establishing the Observant Attention Trait
articles_hidden.authors: Chris Robert Harrison Brown; Vlad Costin; Sophie Forster
articles_hidden.abstract: The characteristic of being observant is a widely acknowledged socio-cultural phenomenon, referring to an individuals’ tendency to be aware of their surrounding environment. However, perhaps due to the lack of a suitable measure, this trait is not yet empirically evidenced or theoretically recognized. Here we sought to empirically establish the construct of an ‘Observant Attention trait’. We developed a novel 19-item self-report measure across multiple large samples (total responses N = 2,441 predominantly undergraduate students). This measure revealed an underlying ‘Observant Attention’ (OA) factor across three sub-factors; specifically, the awareness of subtle details and changes (‘Noticing awareness’), awareness of unexpected motivationally relevant stimuli (‘Alerting awareness’), and awareness of olfactory stimuli (‘Olfactory awareness’). The factor structure and reliability of this model was consistent across multiple samples and confirmed in a pre-registered replication. Test-retest analysis indicated that OA scores remained stable even after a year-long interval. OA showed either no relation to or weak correlations with existing attentional traits, suggesting that it is not adequately indexed by these existing measures, and was also moderately related to patterns of neurodiversity and social distancing failures. OA was only weakly linked to inattentional blindness, consistent with a view that single noticing events may be primarily determined by situational influences, but trait influences may emerge across the countless noticing opportunities that arise within any given day. The current investigation hence provides initial empirical evidence to support the theoretical construct of an Observant Attention Trait, and introduces a reliable measure that enables further study of this trait.

articles_hidden.title: Math Ability Rating Questionnaire (MARQ) for Adults:  Validating a New Self-report Measure
articles_hidden.authors: Daria Khanolainen; Elsje van Bergen; Asko Tolvanen; Tuire Koponen; Jenni Salminen; Minna Torppa; Britt Min; Madelief Isabel Kuijper
articles_hidden.abstract:
From a clinical perspective, identifying individuals with mathematical difficulties is essential for offering support. However, these individuals often avoid mathematical tests due to co-occurring mathematical anxiety. From a research perspective, this leads to systematic data missingness. Moreover, in large-scale research, direct testing is often not feasible because of time and resource constraints. Here, we develop a self-report scale for screening for mathematical difficulties in adults as a cost-effective and time-efficient alternative to mathematical tests. Our mathematical ability rating questionnaire (MARQ) is available in full (19 items) and brief (3 items) versions. The MARQ was developed using a sample of 278 Finnish adults. Participants completed four mathematical tests and filled out a 30-item questionnaire, developed based on extensive literature review. Regression analysis, item response theory, and confirmatory factor analysis were used to identify the items most strongly associated with directly assessed mathematical skills. The full and brief versions of the MARQ had good internal consistency (α = 0.94 and 0.86, respectively) and correlated with mathematical skills (−0.70 and −0.63), mathematical anxiety (0.72 and 0.69), mathematical enjoyment (−0.58 and 0.50), and their children’s mathematical skills (−0.24 and −0.22). The full MARQ accurately identified 93% of adults with higher mathematical skills (test scores above −1 SD) and 52% with lower skills (test scores below −1 SD). A preliminary Dutch replication among university students demonstrated strong internal consistency (α = .86) of the full MARQ but weaker associations with arithmetic fluency (−.23). Overall, the findings support the MARQ as a reliable and scalable tool for assessing self-perceived mathematical ability, particularly in Finnish-speaking populations.
CITE: Khanolainen, D., van Bergen, E., Tolvanen, A., Min, B., Kuijper, M. I., Koponen, T., Salminen, J., & Torppa, M. (in press). Mathematical ability rating questionnaire (MARQ) for adults: Validating a new self-report measure. Journal of Numerical Cognition.

articles_hidden.title: A clinician-informed framework for precision psychotherapy in psychosis
articles_hidden.authors: Shenaya Maria Lisboa; Maria Chiara Del Piccolo; Inês Eulálio; Anna Georgiades; Sandra Vieira
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is the recommended psychosocial intervention for early psychosis;
however, treatment response remains heterogeneous. Precision psychotherapy aims to personalise
treatment by identifying individual characteristics that may predict differential treatment response and
inform treatment selection. However, most precision psychotherapy studies rely on retrospective data
collected using assessment protocols not designed to identify predictors of treatment response and may
therefore fail to capture the full range of characteristics relevant to treatment personalisation. We aimed to
review and expand the current set of predictors used in the literature in CBT from the perspective of
clinicians. Methods. Twenty Clinical Psychologists participated in semi-structured interviews. Clinician-informed predictors were
identified through inductive analysis of unprompted accounts. Clinicians subsequently rated the perceived
importance of these and 32 literature-derived factors on a 10-point scale. Mean ratings and variability were
examined to characterise clinician agreement. Findings were integrated into a candidate predictor
framework linked to available measurement instruments. Results. Clinicians spontaneously identified 38 factors, of which 16 were absent from the literature-derived list.
Factors considered important for engagement with, and benefit from CBTp included cognitive processes,
symptom characteristics, illness history, psychosocial functioning, and migrant status. Clinicians also
identified several under-investigated therapy-related and clinical factors, such as expectations and
understanding of therapy, readiness and motivation for treatment, medication use, level of risk, and
substance misuse. Demographic characteristics more broadly, and basic neurocognitive performance, were
generally considered less important. Conclusion. The resulting clinician-informed framework provides a broader, clinically grounded set of candidate
predictors to inform prospective research into personalised CBTp.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive variability on stable ground:  A narrative review of cognitive fluctuation in childhood and adolescence and hands-on tutorial in quantifying (cognitive) variability
articles_hidden.authors: Jordy van Langen; Michael Aristodemou; Rogier Kievit
articles_hidden.abstract: The importance of cognitive variability in development has been discussed for over a century, but empirical work has lagged behind. However, recent technological and methodological advances have led to a substantial increase in studies focused on cognitive variability in developmental populations. Here we review recent empirical work on cognitive variability during development, examining the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying individual differences and developmental changes in cognitive variability.
